# Mining and Water Quality

[Audio 1](https://smenet.blob.core.windows.net/smecms/sme/media/blobtesteight/miningandwaterquality.mp3)

## Issue

The extraction and processing of mined materials generally require water. Water is also the primary vehicle by which mining-related contaminants can inadvertently be transported into the environment and worsen the quality of water resources. Impacted water quality is a major environmental concern associated with historical and abandoned mines in the U.S. and worldwide. In modern mine planning and permitting, considerable analysis and planning are often required by regulatory agencies during the project design phase to minimize potential impacts to water resources. Prevention of water quality degradation is an important step in ensuring environmental sustainability in mining areas.

## Background

Water use and potential environmental impacts to surface and ground water vary greatly and depend on the size of the mine, its proximity to water resources, the commodity mined (base or precious metals, coal, industrial minerals, aggregates, etc.), the type of deposit (e.g., skarn, porphyry, placer), the method of ore processing (crushing, screening, washing, flotation, leaching), and the mining method (underground, solution, open pit, or dredging). Potential mining-related impacts include both physical and chemical degradation of surface and ground waters. These impacts include sediment discharge and deposition in rivers and lakes and discharges of salty or acidic waters that can often contain dissolved metals and other mine-related constituents.

The legacy of historic mining in the United States is estimated to include more than 500,000 abandoned or inactive mines1. Nearly all of these were operated before modern day mining and environmental controls were instituted. Many of these abandoned mines have the potential for acid generation or other processes that can cause water quality impacts. Internationally, artisanal mining continues to use many of these earlier techniques, creating additional regions of mine-impacted waters.

## Common Water Quality Issues

A major water quality concern related to mining is the formation of acid rock drainage (ARD), sometimes also called acid mine drainage. ARD results from the reaction of water and oxygen with sulfide minerals (pyrite, pyrrhotite, etc.) contained in mined or exposed rock. It leads to acidic waters that mobilize toxic metals, sulfate, and other dissolved solids. When these waters are discharged into surrounding aquifers, lakes, and streams, they can make the water unsafe for people to drink and degrade habitat suitability for aquatic species. Not all types of ore deposits can generate ARD, but metals and other contaminants still can be released.

Another common water quality issue in mining is the physical transport of sediment into water, creating suspended solids. This process can happen as a result of erosion of the ground surface or stored geologic materials. When the amount of suspended solids in water is too high, the water can be less suitable for on-site reuse, requiring more water consumption. When suspended solids are transported to natural waters, they can increase temperature and decrease dissolved oxygen and light penetration, degrading habitat.

The chemicals used in the extraction and processing of ores can also present water quality issues. Although large-scale modern mines carefully manage on-site chemical usage, historic and artisanal mines can release these compounds, such as mercury and cyanide from gold processing.

## Management and Treatment

Important elements of modern mine permitting include assuring the public and government agencies that the potential for water quality impacts is clearly understood and disclosed and that sound water management practices have been incorporated in the planning and design the new mine, including during the pre- and post-mining phases. During operations, mines also have the regulatory and social responsibility to monitor and report on the effectiveness of the water management procedures.

Water discharged from mining operations must meet stringent water quality standards. Federal, state, and local regulations govern mine waste and water management, as well as closure planning and post-closure mitigation and monitoring. Financial assurance requirements have also evolved to better accommodate the known costs of environmental cleanup and mine closure, including any post-closure water treatment requirements, which can be significant and long-term.

Water quality control options can consist of methods to limit reactions between water and mine wastes, manage the flow of potentially impacted waters, and treat impacted waters prior to discharge. Methods that limit the potential for reactions between water and mine wastes include locating mine wastes in areas with limited usable water resources, isolating mine wastes from the environment through the use of liners and caps, and subaqueous disposal of tailings and other mined materials, which uses overlying water to limit the amount of oxygen that can react with the materials. Management of water flow on a mine site can include leachate collection systems, diversion features for run-on and run-off water, and tunnels and cut-offs (e.g., grout curtains or bulkheads) for water within underground workings. Treatment can consist of active measures, such as wastewater treatment plants with reverse osmosis, aeration, or clarification systems, or passive treatments, such as engineered wetlands and reactive barriers or drains. Many of these options can be applied at new and operating mines as well as at historic mines, where they are used by mining companies and government agencies to remediate contamination from historic mining, such as in the stream shown in Figure 1.

## SME Statement of Technical Position

SME supports the goals to continually improve management of water at mines and minimize the effects of mining on water quality by:

*   Preventing or minimizing the generation of acid drainage and the migration of mine-related contaminants to surface and ground water resources;
*   Maximizing water recycling during operations to minimize consumption and discharge; and
*   Integrating pollution prevention and water treatment measures in mine planning and design during the entire mining lifecycle.

These goals can be achieved by:

*   Facilitating research, education, and training in scientific approaches to improving water quality at mining operations;
*   Developing additional water re-use technologies for water encountered at mine sites;
*   Developing mine dewatering approaches that minimize water extraction rates and reduce water quality impacts;

# Mining and Water Quality

[Audio 1](https://smenet.blob.core.windows.net/smecms/sme/media/blobtesteight/miningandwaterquality.mp3)

## Issue

The extraction and processing of mined materials generally require water. Water is also the primary vehicle by which mining-related contaminants can inadvertently be transported into the environment and worsen the quality of water resources. Impacted water quality is a major environmental concern associated with historical and abandoned mines in the U.S. and worldwide. In modern mine planning and permitting, considerable analysis and planning are often required by regulatory agencies during the project design phase to minimize potential impacts to water resources. Prevention of water quality degradation is an important step in ensuring environmental sustainability in mining areas.

## Background

Water use and potential environmental impacts to surface and ground water vary greatly and depend on the size of the mine, its proximity to water resources, the commodity mined (base or precious metals, coal, industrial minerals, aggregates, etc.), the type of deposit (e.g., skarn, porphyry, placer), the method of ore processing (crushing, screening, washing, flotation, leaching), and the mining method (underground, solution, open pit, or dredging). Potential mining-related impacts include both physical and chemical degradation of surface and ground waters. These impacts include sediment discharge and deposition in rivers and lakes and discharges of salty or acidic waters that can often contain dissolved metals and other mine-related constituents.

The legacy of historic mining in the United States is estimated to include more than 500,000 abandoned or inactive mines1. Nearly all of these were operated before modern day mining and environmental controls were instituted. Many of these abandoned mines have the potential for acid generation or other processes that can cause water quality impacts. Internationally, artisanal mining continues to use many of these earlier techniques, creating additional regions of mine-impacted waters.

## Common Water Quality Issues

A major water quality concern related to mining is the formation of acid rock drainage (ARD), sometimes also called acid mine drainage. ARD results from the reaction of water and oxygen with sulfide minerals (pyrite, pyrrhotite, etc.) contained in mined or exposed rock. It leads to acidic waters that mobilize toxic metals, sulfate, and other dissolved solids. When these waters are discharged into surrounding aquifers, lakes, and streams, they can make the water unsafe for people to drink and degrade habitat suitability for aquatic species. Not all types of ore deposits can generate ARD, but metals and other contaminants still can be released.

Another common water quality issue in mining is the physical transport of sediment into water, creating suspended solids. This process can happen as a result of erosion of the ground surface or stored geologic materials. When the amount of suspended solids in water is too high, the water can be less suitable for on-site reuse, requiring more water consumption. When suspended solids are transported to natural waters, they can increase temperature and decrease dissolved oxygen and light penetration, degrading habitat.

The chemicals used in the extraction and processing of ores can also present water quality issues. Although large-scale modern mines carefully manage on-site chemical usage, historic and artisanal mines can release these compounds, such as mercury and cyanide from gold processing.

## Management and Treatment

Important elements of modern mine permitting include assuring the public and government agencies that the potential for water quality impacts is clearly understood and disclosed and that sound water management practices have been incorporated in the planning and design the new mine, including during the pre- and post-mining phases. During operations, mines also have the regulatory and social responsibility to monitor and report on the effectiveness of the water management procedures.

Water discharged from mining operations must meet stringent water quality standards. Federal, state, and local regulations govern mine waste and water management, as well as closure planning and post-closure mitigation and monitoring. Financial assurance requirements have also evolved to better accommodate the known costs of environmental cleanup and mine closure, including any post-closure water treatment requirements, which can be significant and long-term.

Water quality control options can consist of methods to limit reactions between water and mine wastes, manage the flow of potentially impacted waters, and treat impacted waters prior to discharge. Methods that limit the potential for reactions between water and mine wastes include locating mine wastes in areas with limited usable water resources, isolating mine wastes from the environment through the use of liners and caps, and subaqueous disposal of tailings and other mined materials, which uses overlying water to limit the amount of oxygen that can react with the materials. Management of water flow on a mine site can include leachate collection systems, diversion features for run-on and run-off water, and tunnels and cut-offs (e.g., grout curtains or bulkheads) for water within underground workings. Treatment can consist of active measures, such as wastewater treatment plants with reverse osmosis, aeration, or clarification systems, or passive treatments, such as engineered wetlands and reactive barriers or drains. Many of these options can be applied at new and operating mines as well as at historic mines, where they are used by mining companies and government agencies to remediate contamination from historic mining, such as in the stream shown in Figure 1.

## SME Statement of Technical Position

SME supports the goals to continually improve management of water at mines and minimize the effects of mining on water quality by:

*   Preventing or minimizing the generation of acid drainage and the migration of mine-related contaminants to surface and ground water resources;
*   Maximizing water recycling during operations to minimize consumption and discharge; and
*   Integrating pollution prevention and water treatment measures in mine planning and design during the entire mining lifecycle.

These goals can be achieved by:

*   Facilitating research, education, and training in scientific approaches to improving water quality at mining operations;
*   Developing additional water re-use technologies for water encountered at mine sites;
*   Developing mine dewatering approaches that minimize water extraction rates and reduce water quality impacts;
*   Promoting cooperation among international stakeholders engaged in scientific or engineering work in the field of mine water problems and related sciences; and
*   Promoting the exchange and publication of water-related scientific and engineering information.

# Assessing Water-Related Risks in the Mining Sector

Lead PI: 
Unit Affiliation: [Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment (CCSI)](https://people.climate.columbia.edu/units/view/34)

Unknown start date - Ongoing Active [Global](https://people.climate.columbia.edu/projects/showlocation/Global) ; [Chile](https://people.climate.columbia.edu/projects/showlocation/Chile) ; [China](https://people.climate.columbia.edu/projects/showlocation/China) ; [Peru](https://people.climate.columbia.edu/projects/showlocation/Peru) ; [Philippines](https://people.climate.columbia.edu/projects/showlocation/Philippines) ; [South Africa](https://people.climate.columbia.edu/projects/showlocation/South%20Africa) ; [Australia](https://people.climate.columbia.edu/projects/showlocation/Australia) ; [United States](https://people.climate.columbia.edu/projects/showlocation/United%20States) ; [Canada](https://people.climate.columbia.edu/projects/showlocation/Canada) Project Type: Research

**DESCRIPTION:** As populations, economies and global per capita consumption continue to grow, so does the need for raw materials. Mining activity will need to increase to meet these growing demands. At the same time, water availability and poor water quality are increasingly emerging as global risks for many industries, especially in arid and densely populated regions, and the mining sector is no exception. Because of the long-term and potentially irreversible impacts of mineral extraction on land and water resources, the mining sector faces increasing scrutiny from citizens, local and national governments, and civil society organizations.  
 As part of a 3-year grant from Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), CCSI worked with the Columbia Water Center to develop and benchmark a modeling platform for quantitatively assessing the environmental risks associated with gold and copper mining projects and their resulting financial implications.

**OUTCOMES:** For this project, CCSI conducted a review of the legal and regulatory frameworks governing the use and discharge of water by the copper and gold mining sectors in a selected sample of resource rich jurisdictions. An overview of the findings was published in the Resources Policy Journal. Interviews of mining company representatives working on water management issues complement the legal review to highlight the perceived regulatory risk by investors of the analyzed jurisdictions. The countries assessed include Chile, China, Peru, Philippines, South Africa, Australia (Western Australia), United States (Federal, Alaska, Arizona,New Mexico,Nevada), and Canada (British Columbia). The comparative review and profiles are intended as a useful resource for policy makers, researchers and civil society groups seeking to understand and compare how water issues are regulated in the hard rock mining sector in their jurisdictions.  
  
 As part of this project, CCSI also researched whether water-related issues drive social conflicts. A study published in the Resources Policy Journal finds that quality and availability of water have been drivers for water-related social conflicts with mining companies in Peru. However, other factors such as revenue payments to the sub-national level have played a bigger role.   
  
 CCSI organized an event for institutional investors to discuss water related risks from an investor perspective in September 2016 (see background brief here) and co-submitted a letter to the SEC to comment on the modernization of property disclosures for mining companies.   
  
 Furthermore, CCSI has developed a framework to approach the shared use of water and water infrastructure, among other types of infrastructure, after conducting a worldwide survey of related case studies. Research papers on shared use in the context of other types of infrastructure are posted here.

## Abstract

The aim of this study is to characterise environmental impacts associated with mining operations in the Sonora River basin, a water-scarce region of Mexico. The focus is on evaluating water availability, water quality, and sediment composition along the river. Furthermore, the quality of groundwater for human consumption is assessed. Data collected from an extensive field campaign is employed for this purpose. For the first time, measurements of groundwater levels in conjunction with satellite data have shown a substantial decline in groundwater levels in the northern part of the Sonora River basin, near the Buenavista del Cobre mine, highlighting how mining activities are directly affecting the loss of groundwater resources. Results relative to heavy metal pollution in the river’s surface water indicated the presence of hazardous metals at health-concerning concentrations in two areas in the river basin’s central region. Both assessed indices, the contamination degree factor and the Metal Evaluation Index, demonstrated significant heavy metal pollution associated with mining operations. Moreover, the sediment analysis clearly reveals various areas and mechanisms of heavy metal contamination within the watershed. The Pollutant Load Index (PLI) and the Ecological Risk Index (ERI) indicated significant ecological danger and severe contamination near a mine and in two regions where sediment deposition occurs (as evidenced by ERI > 300 and PLI > 3). This suggests a diffusive contamination process that conveys metals from the northern section of the basin to the southern areas of the Sonora River, due to the steeper slopes of upstream rivers. Lastly, groundwater sources intended for human consumption demonstrated generally good to excellent water quality, proving to be unaffected by mining operations. Findings show that in arid regions, it is crucial to regularly revise environmental effects of water-intense mining activities to ensure sustainable water use and to lessen risks to nearby ecosystems and local communities.

## 1 Introduction

Contemporary global society is economically, socially, and culturally dependent on minerals and metals. Production patterns are influenced by the consumption of mineral resources, which is increasing in middle- to high-income nations and attaining historic levels due to the energy transition (Vidal et al., 2013). This situation presents significant challenges for decision-makers and mining companies, since expectations for sustainability across the industry are rising (Gloaguen et al., 2022; Gordon et al., 2006).

For the minerals industry, which is water-intensive, there are two main impacts arising from water consumption. The first is associated with the impacts of quantitative depletion of freshwater within an aquifer or catchment, while the second is related to the degradation of water quality (Prior et al., 2012). A significant number of the world’s largest mineral reserves are located in some of the driest regions on earth (Northey et al., 2014), such as northern of Mexico, which brings a series of major challenges to safeguard operations in an environmentally sustainable manner in regions with high water scarcity (Northey et al., 2017).

In Mexico, most of the mining states are in arid regions, such as Sonora, which has over a century of industrial mining operations. The historical context of mining in this region indicates a trend of environmental impacts resulting from several mining operations and the release of heavy metals into surrounding water bodies (Calmus et al., 2018). For instance, the catastrophic spill from the Buenavista del Cobre mine in August 2014, highlights the severe hazards intrinsic in mining operations. This episode not only polluted the river but also modified the sediment composition, resulting in enduring ecological repercussions (León‐García et al., 2022; Rivera-Uria et al., 2018). On the other hand, many mining operations in the river basin have led to several studies that look at the environmental risks of mining and how it affects river and sediment pollution (Aguilar-Hinojosa et al., 2016; Archundia et al., 2021; Jara-Marini et al., 2023; Mora-Sanchez et al., 2024).

The decline in water quality of the Sonora River, is associated with the influx of heavy metals from mining operations and the inherent geological conditions. The continuous presence of heavy metals including copper, iron and arsenic, in the river system implies significant hazards to aquatic organisms and human health (León‐García et al., 2022; Rivera-Uria et al., 2018; Figueroa-Torres et al., 2014). Communities dependent on the Sonora River for drinking water and agriculture encounter heightened health risks due to contaminated water sources (Rivera-Uria et al., 2018; Valdés-Hernández et al., 2017). Although many studies have shown water quality and metal concentrations in sediments within the Sonora River basin (Aragonés et al., 2017; Guzmán et al., 2019), there is limited evidence concerning the quantitative estimation of groundwater depletion within the aquifers.

The mining industry entails significant water consumption (Northey et al., 2016), potentially resulting in lowered water tables in aquifers (Raghavendra & Deka, 2015). Indeed, some studies show that mining operations in the catchment are among the largest consumers of groundwater in the region, leading to concerns about aquifer depletion and the sustainability of water resources (Díaz Caravantes et al., 2022). Recently, people in the northern region of the Sonora River catchment have expressed environmental concerns regarding groundwater depletion, leading to social instability and protests against certain mines due to the emergence of dry wells in neighbouring towns (Animal Político, 2024; Reyes, 2024).

Several studies have acknowledged the necessity to assess the cumulative impacts of mining operations on the environment (Mudd,2008; Mudd, 2010). In the Sonora River case, in addition to the existing mining operations, there are multiple abandoned mines. However, it is known that these abandoned sites have a low to null impact on the sediment quality, which is attributed to the scarcity of precipitation due to the arid climate of the region (Guzmán et al., 2019). This context highlights the great necessity for continuous monitoring of water and sediments in the basin, along with recurrent measurement of aquifer water levels, to safeguard both the ecosystem health and mining operations in the face of societal discontent (Owen et al., 2023). This will enable a thorough understanding of the long-term consequences of mining and the development of suitable management solutions to alleviate these impacts.

In arid regions, such as the Sonora River basin, it is crucial to evaluate the environmental impacts of water-intensive mining activities on groundwater levels, water quality, and sediments in a comprehensive manner. This study represents the first integrated enterprise aimed at this purpose. The initiative consisted of a comprehensive field campaign conducted between 2021 and 2024 to assess the quality of surface water and groundwater, analyse heavy metal concentrations in sediments, and monitor water levels in aquifers. For the first time in Mexico, total water storage data from the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) mission is used to evaluate the anthropogenic relationship between aquifer depletion and mining activities (Lo et al., 2016).

This work is organised as follows: Section 2 provides a description of the study area; Section 3 introduces the methodology, incorporating a brief description of the selected wells for water table monitoring close to communities and locations for sampling water and sediments along the stream network. Additionally, Section 4 incorporates the results pertaining to changes in groundwater levels, together with data on water quality of the river and drinking wells as well as sediments. Finally, Section 5 introduces the main conclusions and future work.

## 2 Case Study

The selected study area is in the Northwestern Mexican state of Sonora, encompassing the watershed of the Sonora River up to El Molinito Dam (Fig.1). This catchment covers an area of 11,742.35 km 2 and receives an average annual precipitation of 460 mm (Vega-Granillo et al., 2011). The major part of the state is considered arid or semiarid and is characterised by high temperatures and the absence of precipitation during most of the year (Hallack-Alegría & Watkins, 2007). The region displays a biomodal rainfall pattern, with a significant portion of the annual precipitation attributed to the North American monsoon, occurring in the summer (July–September) and a smaller portion occurring during December-January.

## 3 Methodology

Considering the extensive mining operations within the Sonora River basin, the methodology comprises an extensive field campaign (carried out between the years 2021 and 2024) to evaluate the main environmental impacts of this industry, namely groundwater depletion, degradation of river water quality and alterations in sediment quality. Additionally, we integrate the findings from water quality samples conducted in the drinking wells of towns situated along the river course.

### 3.1 Groundwater Measurements

The water balance of an aquifer is influenced by climate, specifically through precipitation and infiltration, as well as the volume of groundwater extractions. Consequently, recharge is a variable influenced by precipitation and infiltration; provided as extractions from wells do not exceed this rate, the aquifer remains in equilibrium. However, if groundwater extraction surpasses recharge, it results in a reduction of stored water volume, leading to depletion.

The depletion of groundwater storage is widely acknowledged as a significant global issue that jeopardises the sustainability of water resources and ecosystems (e.g., Gleeson et al., 2012; Konikow & Kendy, 2005; Schwartz & Ibaraki, 2011).

It is recognised that long-term groundwater depletion is mostly caused by overexploitation, characterised by excessive and unsustainable withdrawals from wells; while, shorter-term local to regional depletion trends may be significantly influenced by natural variability in precipitation and recharge over months to years (Konikow, 2014).

Considering the arid conditions of the Sonora River basin and the extensive mining activities occurring in this region, it is imperative to evaluate the status of water storage in the northern aquifers Bacoachi (orange polygon) and Bacanuchi (blue polygon), as depicted in Fig.2a. To do this, we implemented a water level monitoring campaign. The red dots in Fig.2a indicate the locations of the selected wells in both aquifers, where water level was measured. This comprises 16 wells in the Bacanuchi aquifer and 27 wells in the Bacoachi aquifer. These aquifers are selected since in both cases mining operations use most of the groundwater rights. In the case of the Bacanuchi aquifer, industrial use of groundwater for mining operations accounts for 7.426 Hm 3/year (for clarity: 1 Hm 3 = 10 6 m 3), which represents 57.4% of the total volume authorised for extraction from the aquifer by the National Water Commission. On the other hand, in the Bacoachi aquifer mining operations utilise 16.76 Hm 3/year, which represents 59.7% of the total volume authorised for withdrawal from the aquifer by the National Water Commission (REPDA, 2024). Therefore, any changes seen in water level may be predominantly ascribed to mining operations in this region.

### 3.2 Water Quality in the River

A field campaign was conducted in November 2021 to evaluate the water quality features of the Sonora River. Figure2b illustrates with blue circles the locations of the 17 positions selected within the basin, from the northern region to the Molinito dam. This comprised the sample of tributaries in the northern area of the basin, where Bacoachi stream merges with Bacanuchi river to form the Sonora River next to the town of Arizpe. This involved two sample stations for both streams Bacanuchi (points 1 and 4 in Fig.2b) and Bacoachi (2 and 3 in Fig.2b). Furthermore, two additional locations were detected within the El Molinito dam in the southern region of the basin.

All samples were collected and analysed at the water quality laboratory of the Mexican Institute of Water Technology, which is accredited by the Mexican Accreditation Entity, A.C. (EMA) and approved by the National Water Commission (CONAGUA) under number CNA-GCA-1928, in accordance with the provisions of the Mexican Standard NMX-EC-17025:2018, ensuring that the laboratory and its personnel meet the technical competence criteria for providing technically valid test results. The characteristics evaluated for the water samples from the 17 locations included pH, electrical conductivity, dissolved oxygen, temperature, and heavy metals.

To assess the level of river stream contamination resulting from mining activities, two pollution indices were computed based on the concentration of heavy metals present in water samples. The Contamination Degree (_Cd_) and the Metal Evaluation Index (MEI) which have been effectively employed to assess metal contamination levels arising from mining activities (Bhuiyan et al., 2010a, 2010b; Ayiwouo et al., 2022).

The contamination degree (_Cd_) quantifies the combined impacts of heavy metals concentrations considered hazardous to water (Backman et al., 1998; Edet & Offiong, 2002;). This index is determined using Eqs. (1) and (2):

$$Cd=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{C}_{fi}$$

 (1) 

where

$${C}_{fi}=\left({~}^{{C}_{Oi}}\!\left/ \!{~}_{{C}_{Ni}}\right.\right)-1$$

 (2) 

where _Cd_ is the contamination factor for the i-th metal analysed, _C_ _Oi_ denotes the observed concentration value for the i-th metal, and _C_ _Ni_ is the upper permissible concentration established by environmental regulations and standards for the i-th metal. This research employs the official criteria for the protection of aquatic life in water bodies issued by the Mexican government (CONAGUA, 2023). This parameter may be classified as follows: Low pollution (_Cd_< 1); medium pollution (1 <_Cd_< 3) and highly polluted (_Cd_> 3).

The second index refers to the Metal Evaluation Index (MEI) employed to also evaluate heavy metal contamination in surface water. Following Edet and Offiong (2002), it offers a more accurate evaluation through the identification of the degree of metal contamination in water. It is calculated with Eq. (3):

$$MEI=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{~}^{{H}_{C}}\!\left/ \!{~}_{{H}_{MAC} }\right.$$

 (3) 

where H C and H MAC are the measured values for each detected metal and the maximum admissible concentration (MAC) of the i-th metal, respectively (see Table1). The MEI values are divided into 3 pollution classes: Low pollution (MEI < 5); medium pollution (MEI 5–20) and highly polluted (MEI > 20).

### 3.3 Sediments

To assess the sediment quality throughout the basin, two sample campaigns were conducted: the first in July 2021, encompassing 18 sites along the river, and the second in November 2021, comprising 8 sites determined in collaboration with community members. Thus, results comprise information from 26 locations along the Sonora River, extending from its northern region near the Buenavista del Cobre mine to the southernmost point at the El Molinito dam, as indicated by the orange dots in Fig.2c. Notably, during the July 2021 sampling, a few dry sediment samples were collected at locations in proximity to the Buenavista del Cobre mine, as denoted in Fig.2c by points 1 and 2.

The sediments were examined at the laboratory of the Mexican Institute of Water Technology, where the analysis encompassed the detection and identification of the following heavy metals: aluminum (Al), antimony (Sb), arsenic (As), barium (Ba), copper (Cu), iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), lead (Pb), and zinc (Zn).

Several pollution indicators were used in this assessment to determine the level of heavy metal contamination in the Sonora River Basin’s surface sediments. The indicators comprise the contamination factor (_CF_), ecological risk index (_ERI_), and pollution load index (_PLI_). These indices are employed to assess the enrichment of metals relative to baseline values (Areguamen et al., 2023).

The contamination factor (_CF_) is determined using the equation:

$$CF={~}^{{C}_{m}}\!\left/ \!{~}_{{C}_{b}}\right.$$

 (4) 

where _C_ _m_ denotes the concentration of the metal in the analysed sediment sample and _C_ _b_ indicates the baseline level derived from geological charts issued by the Mexican Geological Service for this watershed (Servicio Geológico Mexicano, 1999&2021). Background values of each metal are reported in Table1. The _CF_ is categorised into five classifications, from pure to severely contaminated sediments.

The ecological risk index (_ERI_), as proposed by Håkanson (1980), is employed to evaluate the degree of ecological risk posed by heavy metals and is defined with the following equation:

$$ERI=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{E}_{ri}$$

 (5) 

where _E_ _ri_ denotes the risk factor for the i-th detected metal and is determined by multiplying _CF_ (Eq.4) by the toxicity response coefficient (_Tr_ _i_) for each element. The dimensionless toxicity response coefficients for the seven metals found in the samples are allocated as follows: As = 10, Pb = Cu = Ni = 5 and Mn = Fe = Zn = 1, as established in previous research (Abdel-Raheem et al., 2024; Cheng & Yap, 2015; Håkanson, 1980). The _ERI_ values are classified into five categories, from low to hazardous risk.

Tomlinson et al. (1980) defined the pollutant load index (_PLI_), which is used to assess the level of contamination in sediments. The calculation is performed using the subsequent equation:

$$PLI=\sqrt[n]{{CF}_{1}\times {CF}_{2}\times {CF}_{3}\times \dots \times {CF}_{n}}$$

 (6) 

where _CF_ denotes the contamination factor and _n_ signifies the quantity of detected metals. The _PLI_ is classified into five categories, from optimal to extreme heavy metal contamination. The pollutant load index is classified into four categories, such as _PLI_< 1, no pollution; 1 <_PLI_< 2, moderate pollution; 2 <_PLI_< 3, heavy pollution; and 3 <_PLI_, extreme pollution.

### 3.4 Drinking Water Wells

Numerous reports indicate elevated arsenic levels in groundwater across the dry and semi-arid regions of northern Mexico, such as in the Sonora River basin, primarily attributed to geogenic, mining, and thermal sources (Alarcón-Herrera et al., 2020; Osuna-Martínez et al., 2021). Consequently, this study also included the evaluation of water quality in wells that provide water supply to the principal towns along the Sonora River. Considering that groundwater is the principal supply of drinking water, it is imperative to conduct research that assesses the evolution of water quality in these sources. Consequently, two more field campaigns were executed in November 2021 and February 2023, involving the sampling of 28 wells selected in conjunction with community leaders, illustrated in Fig.2d with blue diamonds.

All samples were examined at the water quality laboratory of the Mexican Institute of Water Technology, encompassing pH, electrical conductivity, dissolved oxygen, temperature, and heavy metals. Results were evaluated against the health guidelines for drinking water outlined in norm NOM-127-SSA1-2021, which stipulates the acceptable quality standards that water must fulfil for human use and consumption.

Moreover, to evaluate the overall water quality in drinking wells and the viability of using it for human consumption we utilize the Water Quality Index (Štambuk-Giljanović, 1999). This index allows the reduction of several measurable parameters into a single value. Its estimation comprises five steps as follows: (1) assigning weight to each detected parameter (w _i_), (2) relative weight (W i), (3) quality rating (_q_ _i_), (4) sub-index (SI i) and (5) summation of sub-index (_WQI_) (Ayiwouo, et al., 2022).

To calculate the _WQI_ of drinking water, each parameter was defined by given a certain numeric value, i.e. assigning weights (w i), in a range of 1 (least) to 5 (highest). The ranking is based on the parameter importance to the water quality, where the maximum weight of ‘‘5’’ was designated to the most harmful parameters (Varol & Davraz, 2015). Second, the relative weight (W i) of each parameter was computed using Eq. (7):

$${W}_{i}=\frac{{w}_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w}_{i}}$$

 (7) 

where _W_ _i_ is the relative weight, _w_ _i_ the weight of the parameter, and _n_ the number of parameters. The quality rating (_q_ _i_) of each parameter is estimated using the following equation:

$${q}_{i}=\frac{{C}_{i}}{{S}_{i}}\times 100$$

 (8) 

Where Ci is the measured concentration (mg/l) of each parameter in each water sample, Si the drinking water standard (mg/l) as defined in the Mexican regulation for water for human consumption NOM127-SSA1-2021. The sub-index Sli was estimated for each parameter using:

$${Sl}_{i}={W}_{i}\times {q}_{i}$$

 (9) 

The sum of the subindex _Sl_ _i_ of all analysed parameters provides the value of _WQI_ and is defined by:

$$WQI=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{Sl}_{i}$$

 (10) 

The Water Quality Index (_WQI_) estimation in this study was derived from twelve distinct parameters, along with their respective weights and relative importance to human health. This index is categorised into five classifications (Şener et al., 2017): Excellent (< 50); good (50–100); poor (100–200); very bad (200–300); and unfit for consumption (> 300).

## 4 Results and Discussion

### 4.1 Groundwater Levels

Results concerning the long-term trends in the evolution of piezometric levels in the Bacanuchi and Bacoachi aquifers are presented. This involves the calculation of changes in water levels recorded during our field campaign in February 2024 compared to data collected in previous years (2005 and 2016). Table 2 displays the measurement findings for the Bacanuchi aquifer, together with data related to elevations, water depths and differences in water level between years. In this aquifer, of the 16 wells measured in 2024, 4 are newly established wells that had not been previously measured, while the remaining wells have historical data from prior years. Table 2 indicates a general decline in aquifer levels by 2024. The most significant reductions are located in the northern region, particularly adjacent to the extraction zone of the Buenavista del Cobre mining operation near the city of Cananea.

Recorded data from both aquifers reveal sustained depletion trends over time, however, the observed decline in water levels can also be partially attributed to regional drought conditions (e.g. Moran et al., 2022), which may intensify current water stress. To evaluate the anthropogenic link between aquifer depletion and mining operations, an additional analysis utilising total water storage data from the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) mission is also provided (Lo et al., 2016; Rodell et al., 2009; Wada et al., 2010). Figure3 illustrates the time series of total water storage anomaly in panel (a) (where red and blue stripes denote negative and positive anomalies, respectively, with darker hues indicating greater anomalies). Panel (b) presents the temporal variation of the percentage area of the upper Sonora River basin subject to drought conditions, with darker warm hues indicating more severe drought intensity, whereas panel (c) illustrates the annual copper production by the Buenavista del Cobre mine. These graphs clearly show that during years 2002–2006, when copper production at Buenavista de Cobre was approximately 120,000 tonnes annually, the total water storage anomaly identified by the GRACE mission fluctuated around zero (with contrasting blue and very light red colors), indicating a balance between groundwater extraction and recharge in this region. This trend persisted throughout the Cananea strike (2007–2010), which forced the cessation of production at the mine. The data in panel (a) illustrates a distinct declining trend beginning in 2011 (in light red color), coinciding with the mine’s reopening and a rise in production to roughly 320,000 tonnes of copper annually. Additionally, a subsequent decline in total water storage is illustrated in 2020 (in darker red), coinciding with a further increase in copper production to 450,000 tonnes per year. Significantly, severe drought conditions were observed in both 2011 and 2021 (panel b). This finding suggests that there is, in fact, a feedback loop between the water-intensive mining activities that are depleting both aquifers and the occurred drought conditions. Severe drought conditions were recorded in both 2006 and 2014, as illustrated in panel (b) of the figure. However, in these circumstances, the aquifer seems to recuperate following the cessation of drought conditions, as evidenced by the anomaly of total water storage depicted in panel (a) (blue colours post-2006, and light red colours post-2014 in panel a). The persistent decline in total water storage recorded by GRACE from 2011, may primarily be ascribed to the increase of copper production at the mine over the years 2011 and 2020. This rise in production requires significantly more water, and while drought conditions may exacerbate the reduction in water availability, the primary driving factor seems to be the extraction of water from the aquifer.

As it was reported, industrial groundwater use for mining operations at Buenavista del Cobre accounts for 57.4% of the extraction volume authorised from the Bacanuchi aquifer and 59.7% of the total withdrawal volume permitted from the Bacoachi aquifer. Despite several water users exist within both aquifers (including livestock, agricultural and domestic users), no single user has access to the entire volume of water, since it is allocated among various water rights holders. Agriculture constitutes 39% of water extractions in Bacanuchi, including 27 water right holders, and 14% in Bacoachi, with 80 water right holders (REPDA, 2024). The observed reduction in water levels and total water storage from GRACE, can mostly be ascribed to mining activities (e.g. Jódar et al., 2024).

Therefore, it is crucial to develop improved strategies for managing groundwater extractions resulting from mining activities to maintain well water levels for the community. The depletion of aquifers resulting from mining operations is a major environmental issue. Effective management measures are essential to mitigate the impacts on groundwater resources. Among the best management practices is gangue backfilling in mining, which can mitigate the risk of overburden aquifer degradation (Ma et al., 2020). In arid regions, techniques such as infiltration basins or bore injection are used to replenish aquifers, serving as strategies for managing aquifer recharge that reduce groundwater impacts and expedite recovery post-mining, provided they are carefully planned (Alam et al., 2021; Cook et al., 2022; Sloan et al., 2023).

In regions such as Sonora, marked by considerable water scarcity, it is anticipated that a reduced extraction rate, along with increased input through managed aquifer recharge techniques, can alleviate groundwater depletion and achieve long-term sustainability (Tewari et al., 2024). Therefore, the strategic planning of water extraction and the execution of integrated management approaches for mining operations may contribute to preserving aquifer integrity and ensuring sustainable water resource management in this region.

### 4.2 Water Quality in the River

The amounts of heavy metals in water samples collected along the river channel are presented in Table4. Traces of Al, As, Fe, Mn, Hg, and Zn are evident at all locations throughout the river course. Measured concentrations for Al, Fe, Mn and Zn do not comply with official criteria for the protection of aquatic life in water bodies, as issued by the Mexican government. Mining activities release pollutants through several primary pathways, adversely affecting the ecosystem. These mechanisms encompass water contamination and soil pollution. The primary mechanisms of pollutant release are acid mine drainage, caused by the oxidative dissolution of sulphide minerals, which introduces acidic water rich in heavy metals into adjacent water bodies (Simate and Ndlovu, 2014), as examined in this river by Mora-Sánchez et al. (2024) and Rivera-Uria et al. (2018). Furthermore, leachate from mining tailings ponds may introduce contaminants into groundwater (Ali et al., 2023), while insufficient waste management might result in heavy metal pollution. Moreover, the failure of tailings dams has been demonstrated to significantly contaminate rivers (Pacheco et al., 2022, 2023). Nonetheless, in the absence of catastrophic collapses, tailings dams can contribute to long-term pollution of river systems. Research indicates that metal mining activities, particularly tailings storage, impact vast river channels and floodplains worldwide, with common pollutants including lead, zinc, copper, and arsenic (Kossoff et al., 2014; Macklin et al., 2023).

Regarding the Sonora River, while there have been no failures of tailing dam facilities per se, acid mine drainage systems have malfunctioned during tropical storms, resulting in the release of heavy metals into the river, as documented in September 2014 during Hurricane Odile, following the notable incident of August 2014 (Calderón, 2014).

To prevent pollution due to acid mine drainage the construction of wetlands and limestone drains has been suggested as well as the enhancement of environmental standards and regulations for the mining sector to reduce pollution resulting from mining activities (RoyChowdhury et al., 2015; Dehkordi et al., 2024). Additionally, robust enforcement and implementation of environmental regulations and standards are essential for effective pollution control (Agboola et al., 2020).

### 4.3 Sediments

Soils are the major sink for heavy metals released into the environment by anthropogenic activities and do not experience microbial or chemical degradation, leading to prolonged persistence of their total concentration in soils following their introduction (Adriano, 2003). Sediments may become contaminated by the accumulation of heavy metals through emissions from industrial areas, mine tailings, disposal of high metal wastes, land application of fertilizers, animal manures, sewage sludge, pesticides, among others (Wuana & Okieimen, 2011).

The predominant industrial activity in the Sonora River basin is mining. Consequently, 26 distinct locations were chosen to evaluate the level of sediment pollution along the river’s course. The findings from the sample analyses are displayed in Table7, accompanied by the coordinates of each sampling site. High quantities of Al, Sb, As, Ba, Cu, Fe, Mn, Hg, Ni, Pb, and Zn are detected at multiple locations along the river, whereas values for Cd and Cr are undetected at most locations.

These results distinctly emphasise various areas and mechanisms of heavy metal contamination within the watershed. At point 2, adjacent to the Buenavista del Cobre mine, the indices reveal significant ecological risk and extreme contamination, due to the site’s proximity to a large tailings complex. This result aligns with findings from a prior study (conducted ten years ago) in the region, which indicated severe contamination and considerable environmental risk (Aguilar-Hinojosa, et al., 2016). Our findings confirm that both severe contamination and elevated ecological risk persist in the area due to mining operations.

Furthermore, point 1, located within the Bacanuchi river network and near tailings facilities of the same mine, has moderate pollution levels as indicated by the Pollutant Load Index (PLI) and moderate ecological risk according to the Ecological Risk Index (ERI). Point 3, located in the Bacanuchi River downstream of the tailings facilities, demonstrates significant ecological danger and severe contamination, hence validating the results from the water samples which showed high concentration of heavy metals in this river. The higher transport capacity of this stream is ascribed to its steeper slope s = 0.0046, which is determined by its length of 102.05 km and an elevation difference of 841 m from its origin to Arizpe, whereas the Bacoachi stream exhibits a milder slope S = 0.0028 with a longer length of 130.63 km and a height difference of 867 m.

The high concentration of metals in sediments at locations 8 and 13 as indicated by both the ERI and PLI indices, can be attributed to sediment deposition caused by a change in river slope. In the town of Arizpe, where Bacanuchi and Bacoachi streams converge to create the Sonora River, the river flows downstream via a milder slope of S = 0.001. This enables the sediment accumulation at this site, leading to moderate ecological risk indicated by ERI > 300 and extreme contamination defined by PLI > 3.

Further results downstream the river at point 13, indicate an additional site of high metal concentrations in sediments exhibiting comparable values ERI and PLI. This implies a diffusive contamination process that conveys metals from the northern basin, specifically from the Bacanuchi and Bacoachi rivers with steeper gradients, to the southern regions of the Sonora River. Sediments are conveyed along the river and deposited in areas with gentle slopes and limited sediment transport capacity, promoting deposition and the gradual accumulation of metals over time.

The proximity of specific sample locations to the mining operations inevitably results in an increased impact from mining activities (refer to Fig.2c). The findings demonstrate that elevated metal concentrations in sediments in the middle basin are influenced by sediment transport and deposition, suggesting that metals in the Sonora River are dispersing from north to south in alignment with the flow. The results from the pollutant load index at points 24 and 26 (_PLI_> 1), near El Molinito Dam and away from any active mines, indicate that metals are slowly building up due to sediment transport. This hypothesis is corroborated by the contamination degree factor reported in Table8 for Cu, Fe, Ni, and Zn (_CF_> 1) at point 24 and for As and Mn (_CF_> 2) at point 26.

The findings clearly demonstrate that the Sonora River basin is impacted in some areas by heavy metal pollution due to mining operations, adversely influencing sediment and surface water quality. The high pollutant load index PLI at certain locations of the river (points 8 and 13), indicates the transport of heavy metals via sediment, while the contamination factor (CF) values for certain metals at these sites reveal the influence of anthropogenic activities. At point 8, CF > 1 are noted for As, Mn, Ni and Zn, whereas at point 13 values of CF > 1 are registered for As, Cu, Pb and Zn. These results align with those previously documented by Jara-Marini et al. (2023) who also showed large contamination factors for Mn, Pb and Zn. Moreover, the results found in point 13 are in accordance to those found by Mora-Sánchez et al. (2024), who analysed the mobility of toxic metals from an abandoned tailing deposit located 1.5 km from the Sonora River in the town of San Felipe de Jesús.

## 5 Conclusions

This study introduced results of an extensive field campaign conducted in the Sonora River basin carried out between 2021 and 2024, aimed at characterising environmental impacts of mining operations on groundwater levels, water quality and sediments along the river. Furthermore, to assess the water quality for human consumption, results from groundwater wells throughout the river course were also presented. Field studies of groundwater levels, in conjunction with GRACE satellite data, revealed a significant decline in levels in both the Bacoachi and Bacanuchi aquifers in the northern region of the Sonora River basin. This depletion was associated with mining operations confirming a human-induced drop in groundwater availability. Furthermore, a feedback loop between the water-intensive mining and the prevailing drought conditions was examined, revealing that prior to 2011, the aquifer could recuperate after the cessation of drought conditions. The ongoing reduction in total water storage observed since 2011 can be mostly attributed to the rise in copper production at the mine between 2011 and 2020. Although drought conditions may intensify the decrease in water availability, the primary driving factor appears to be withdrawal of water from the aquifer for mining purposes. Negative variations in water levels significantly affect the wells located in the northern regions of both aquifers, near the Buenavista del Cobre mine. The mine holds more than 55% of water rights and accounts for the majority of water volume extractions in both aquifers, demonstrating a direct effect of mining operations on the depletion of groundwater supplies.

Analysis of the river water samples revealed the presence of harmful heavy metals in surface water at levels that pose health risk. This was particularly evident in two primary regions within the central part of the river basin, where both the contamination degree factor and the Metal Evaluation Index, identified heavy metal contamination. Moreover, at locations along the Bacanuchi River downstream from two major tailing dams of Buenavista del Cobre mine, there were notable indications of contamination.

The results clearly highlight different regions and processes of heavy metal pollution in the watershed concerning sediments. We employed the Pollutant Load Index (PLI) and the Ecological Risk Index (ERI), both of which identified a significant ecological risk and extreme contamination in an area next to the Buenavista del Cobre mine and its tailings complex. Points located in the Bacanuchi stream exhibited a significant ecological danger and severe contamination, corroborated by the water sample analyses from that river. As indicated by prior studies (Miller, 1997; Qiao et al., 2023), the presence of metals can be ascribed to the increased transport capacity in catchments exhibiting a steeper landscape and fluvial characteristics, as observed in Bacanuchi. Additionally, two areas with elevated concentrations of heavy metals in sediments were found in both the ERI and PLI indices. Sediment deposition occurs in these places due to a change of slope, facilitating sediment accumulation and resulting in moderate ecological risk indicated by ERI > 300 and extreme contamination characterised by PLI > 3. This suggest a diffusive contamination process that transports metals from the northern part of the basin, specifically from the Bacanuchi and Bacoachi rivers with steeper gradients, to the southern regions of the Sonora River. Sediments are transported by the river and deposited in regions with mild slopes and limited sediment transport capacity, facilitating deposition and the gradual accumulation of metals over time. The results clearly demonstrate that certain regions of the Sonora River basin are affected by heavy metal pollution stemming from mining activities, adversely influencing sediment and surface water quality. The contamination factor (CF) values for certain metals revealed the influence of anthropogenic activities. Specifically, at point 8, CF > 1 was seen for As, Mn, Ni and Zn, while at point 13 values of CF > 1 are registered for As, Cu, Pb and Zn.

Even in the absence of significant failures of tailings facilities, it has been demonstrated that harmful compounds emitted from acid mine drainage and leaks from mining tailings ponds contribute to persistent river contamination. While many mines have commenced enhancements to their tailings dam structures and acid mine drainage systems, it is equally imperative to address pollution through the construction of wetlands and limestone drains, alongside the strengthening of environmental legislation governing the mining sector. In 2023, Mexico’s Congress introduced a new mining law to enhance environmental protection for natural reserves by requiring companies to present closure, post-closure, and restoration programs for mines in compliance with international standards.

Finally, groundwater sources intended for human consumption exhibited good to excellent water quality (WQI < 100), with the exception of two sites indicating poor quality (100 > WQI > 200) and one location where the water is considered unfit for consumption (WQI > 300). Consequently, results from this investigation indicate that the water intended for human use from studied groundwater wells is considered safe and unimpacted by mining activities.

Our research demonstrates that in the Sonora River basin, both current and past mining operations, along with varying hydrological conditions, have adversely affected surface water quality and groundwater quantity, presenting considerable environmental threats to riparian ecosystems and local communities. Consequently, mining operations are encouraged to implement a strategic plan for water extraction over time, coupled with enhanced input via managed aquifer recharge techniques, to avert societal discontent due to excessive extraction and to attain long-term sustainability in their operations.

## Abstract

The aim of this study is to characterise environmental impacts associated with mining operations in the Sonora River basin, a water-scarce region of Mexico. The focus is on evaluating water availability, water quality, and sediment composition along the river. Furthermore, the quality of groundwater for human consumption is assessed. Data collected from an extensive field campaign is employed for this purpose. For the first time, measurements of groundwater levels in conjunction with satellite data have shown a substantial decline in groundwater levels in the northern part of the Sonora River basin, near the Buenavista del Cobre mine, highlighting how mining activities are directly affecting the loss of groundwater resources. Results relative to heavy metal pollution in the river’s surface water indicated the presence of hazardous metals at health-concerning concentrations in two areas in the river basin’s central region. Both assessed indices, the contamination degree factor and the Metal Evaluation Index, demonstrated significant heavy metal pollution associated with mining operations. Moreover, the sediment analysis clearly reveals various areas and mechanisms of heavy metal contamination within the watershed. The Pollutant Load Index (PLI) and the Ecological Risk Index (ERI) indicated significant ecological danger and severe contamination near a mine and in two regions where sediment deposition occurs (as evidenced by ERI > 300 and PLI > 3). This suggests a diffusive contamination process that conveys metals from the northern section of the basin to the southern areas of the Sonora River, due to the steeper slopes of upstream rivers. Lastly, groundwater sources intended for human consumption demonstrated generally good to excellent water quality, proving to be unaffected by mining operations. Findings show that in arid regions, it is crucial to regularly revise environmental effects of water-intense mining activities to ensure sustainable water use and to lessen risks to nearby ecosystems and local communities.

## 1 Introduction

Contemporary global society is economically, socially, and culturally dependent on minerals and metals. Production patterns are influenced by the consumption of mineral resources, which is increasing in middle- to high-income nations and attaining historic levels due to the energy transition (Vidal et al., 2013). This situation presents significant challenges for decision-makers and mining companies, since expectations for sustainability across the industry are rising (Gloaguen et al., 2022; Gordon et al., 2006).

For the minerals industry, which is water-intensive, there are two main impacts arising from water consumption. The first is associated with the impacts of quantitative depletion of freshwater within an aquifer or catchment, while the second is related to the degradation of water quality (Prior et al., 2012). A significant number of the world’s largest mineral reserves are located in some of the driest regions on earth (Northey et al., 2014), such as northern of Mexico, which brings a series of major challenges to safeguard operations in an environmentally sustainable manner in regions with high water scarcity (Northey et al., 2017).

In Mexico, most of the mining states are in arid regions, such as Sonora, which has over a century of industrial mining operations. The historical context of mining in this region indicates a trend of environmental impacts resulting from several mining operations and the release of heavy metals into surrounding water bodies (Calmus et al., 2018). For instance, the catastrophic spill from the Buenavista del Cobre mine in August 2014, highlights the severe hazards intrinsic in mining operations. This episode not only polluted the river but also modified the sediment composition, resulting in enduring ecological repercussions (León‐García et al., 2022; Rivera-Uria et al., 2018). On the other hand, many mining operations in the river basin have led to several studies that look at the environmental risks of mining and how it affects river and sediment pollution (Aguilar-Hinojosa et al., 2016; Archundia et al., 2021; Jara-Marini et al., 2023; Mora-Sanchez et al., 2024).

The decline in water quality of the Sonora River, is associated with the influx of heavy metals from mining operations and the inherent geological conditions. The continuous presence of heavy metals including copper, iron and arsenic, in the river system implies significant hazards to aquatic organisms and human health (León‐García et al., 2022; Rivera-Uria et al., 2018; Figueroa-Torres et al., 2014). Communities dependent on the Sonora River for drinking water and agriculture encounter heightened health risks due to contaminated water sources (Rivera-Uria et al., 2018; Valdés-Hernández et al., 2017). Although many studies have shown water quality and metal concentrations in sediments within the Sonora River basin (Aragonés et al., 2017; Guzmán et al., 2019), there is limited evidence concerning the quantitative estimation of groundwater depletion within the aquifers.

The mining industry entails significant water consumption (Northey et al., 2016), potentially resulting in lowered water tables in aquifers (Raghavendra & Deka, 2015). Indeed, some studies show that mining operations in the catchment are among the largest consumers of groundwater in the region, leading to concerns about aquifer depletion and the sustainability of water resources (Díaz Caravantes et al., 2022). Recently, people in the northern region of the Sonora River catchment have expressed environmental concerns regarding groundwater depletion, leading to social instability and protests against certain mines due to the emergence of dry wells in neighbouring towns (Animal Político, 2024; Reyes, 2024).

Several studies have acknowledged the necessity to assess the cumulative impacts of mining operations on the environment (Mudd,2008; Mudd, 2010). In the Sonora River case, in addition to the existing mining operations, there are multiple abandoned mines. However, it is known that these abandoned sites have a low to null impact on the sediment quality, which is attributed to the scarcity of precipitation due to the arid climate of the region (Guzmán et al., 2019). This context highlights the great necessity for continuous monitoring of water and sediments in the basin, along with recurrent measurement of aquifer water levels, to safeguard both the ecosystem health and mining operations in the face of societal discontent (Owen et al., 2023). This will enable a thorough understanding of the long-term consequences of mining and the development of suitable management solutions to alleviate these impacts.

In arid regions, such as the Sonora River basin, it is crucial to evaluate the environmental impacts of water-intensive mining activities on groundwater levels, water quality, and sediments in a comprehensive manner. This study represents the first integrated enterprise aimed at this purpose. The initiative consisted of a comprehensive field campaign conducted between 2021 and 2024 to assess the quality of surface water and groundwater, analyse heavy metal concentrations in sediments, and monitor water levels in aquifers. For the first time in Mexico, total water storage data from the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) mission is used to evaluate the anthropogenic relationship between aquifer depletion and mining activities (Lo et al., 2016).

This work is organised as follows: Section 2 provides a description of the study area; Section 3 introduces the methodology, incorporating a brief description of the selected wells for water table monitoring close to communities and locations for sampling water and sediments along the stream network. Additionally, Section 4 incorporates the results pertaining to changes in groundwater levels, together with data on water quality of the river and drinking wells as well as sediments. Finally, Section 5 introduces the main conclusions and future work.

## 2 Case Study

The selected study area is in the Northwestern Mexican state of Sonora, encompassing the watershed of the Sonora River up to El Molinito Dam (Fig.1). This catchment covers an area of 11,742.35 km 2 and receives an average annual precipitation of 460 mm (Vega-Granillo et al., 2011). The major part of the state is considered arid or semiarid and is characterised by high temperatures and the absence of precipitation during most of the year (Hallack-Alegría & Watkins, 2007). The region displays a biomodal rainfall pattern, with a significant portion of the annual precipitation attributed to the North American monsoon, occurring in the summer (July–September) and a smaller portion occurring during December-January.

## 3 Methodology

Considering the extensive mining operations within the Sonora River basin, the methodology comprises an extensive field campaign (carried out between the years 2021 and 2024) to evaluate the main environmental impacts of this industry, namely groundwater depletion, degradation of river water quality and alterations in sediment quality. Additionally, we integrate the findings from water quality samples conducted in the drinking wells of towns situated along the river course.

### 3.1 Groundwater Measurements

The water balance of an aquifer is influenced by climate, specifically through precipitation and infiltration, as well as the volume of groundwater extractions. Consequently, recharge is a variable influenced by precipitation and infiltration; provided as extractions from wells do not exceed this rate, the aquifer remains in equilibrium. However, if groundwater extraction surpasses recharge, it results in a reduction of stored water volume, leading to depletion.

The depletion of groundwater storage is widely acknowledged as a significant global issue that jeopardises the sustainability of water resources and ecosystems (e.g., Gleeson et al., 2012; Konikow & Kendy, 2005; Schwartz & Ibaraki, 2011).

It is recognised that long-term groundwater depletion is mostly caused by overexploitation, characterised by excessive and unsustainable withdrawals from wells; while, shorter-term local to regional depletion trends may be significantly influenced by natural variability in precipitation and recharge over months to years (Konikow, 2014).

Considering the arid conditions of the Sonora River basin and the extensive mining activities occurring in this region, it is imperative to evaluate the status of water storage in the northern aquifers Bacoachi (orange polygon) and Bacanuchi (blue polygon), as depicted in Fig.2a. To do this, we implemented a water level monitoring campaign. The red dots in Fig.2a indicate the locations of the selected wells in both aquifers, where water level was measured. This comprises 16 wells in the Bacanuchi aquifer and 27 wells in the Bacoachi aquifer. These aquifers are selected since in both cases mining operations use most of the groundwater rights. In the case of the Bacanuchi aquifer, industrial use of groundwater for mining operations accounts for 7.426 Hm 3/year (for clarity: 1 Hm 3 = 10 6 m 3), which represents 57.4% of the total volume authorised for extraction from the aquifer by the National Water Commission. On the other hand, in the Bacoachi aquifer mining operations utilise 16.76 Hm 3/year, which represents 59.7% of the total volume authorised for withdrawal from the aquifer by the National Water Commission (REPDA, 2024). Therefore, any changes seen in water level may be predominantly ascribed to mining operations in this region.

### 3.2 Water Quality in the River

A field campaign was conducted in November 2021 to evaluate the water quality features of the Sonora River. Figure2b illustrates with blue circles the locations of the 17 positions selected within the basin, from the northern region to the Molinito dam. This comprised the sample of tributaries in the northern area of the basin, where Bacoachi stream merges with Bacanuchi river to form the Sonora River next to the town of Arizpe. This involved two sample stations for both streams Bacanuchi (points 1 and 4 in Fig.2b) and Bacoachi (2 and 3 in Fig.2b). Furthermore, two additional locations were detected within the El Molinito dam in the southern region of the basin.

All samples were collected and analysed at the water quality laboratory of the Mexican Institute of Water Technology, which is accredited by the Mexican Accreditation Entity, A.C. (EMA) and approved by the National Water Commission (CONAGUA) under number CNA-GCA-1928, in accordance with the provisions of the Mexican Standard NMX-EC-17025:2018, ensuring that the laboratory and its personnel meet the technical competence criteria for providing technically valid test results. The characteristics evaluated for the water samples from the 17 locations included pH, electrical conductivity, dissolved oxygen, temperature, and heavy metals.

To assess the level of river stream contamination resulting from mining activities, two pollution indices were computed based on the concentration of heavy metals present in water samples. The Contamination Degree (_Cd_) and the Metal Evaluation Index (MEI) which have been effectively employed to assess metal contamination levels arising from mining activities (Bhuiyan et al., 2010a, 2010b; Ayiwouo et al., 2022).

The contamination degree (_Cd_) quantifies the combined impacts of heavy metals concentrations considered hazardous to water (Backman et al., 1998; Edet & Offiong, 2002;). This index is determined using Eqs. (1) and (2):

$$Cd=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{C}_{fi}$$

 (1) 

where

$${C}_{fi}=\left({~}^{{C}_{Oi}}\!\left/ \!{~}_{{C}_{Ni}}\right.\right)-1$$

 (2) 

where _Cd_ is the contamination factor for the i-th metal analysed, _C_ _Oi_ denotes the observed concentration value for the i-th metal, and _C_ _Ni_ is the upper permissible concentration established by environmental regulations and standards for the i-th metal. This research employs the official criteria for the protection of aquatic life in water bodies issued by the Mexican government (CONAGUA, 2023). This parameter may be classified as follows: Low pollution (_Cd_< 1); medium pollution (1 <_Cd_< 3) and highly polluted (_Cd_> 3).

The second index refers to the Metal Evaluation Index (MEI) employed to also evaluate heavy metal contamination in surface water. Following Edet and Offiong (2002), it offers a more accurate evaluation through the identification of the degree of metal contamination in water. It is calculated with Eq. (3):

$$MEI=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{~}^{{H}_{C}}\!\left/ \!{~}_{{H}_{MAC} }\right.$$

 (3) 

where H C and H MAC are the measured values for each detected metal and the maximum admissible concentration (MAC) of the i-th metal, respectively (see Table1). The MEI values are divided into 3 pollution classes: Low pollution (MEI < 5); medium pollution (MEI 5–20) and highly polluted (MEI > 20).
