### Objectives

There is a patchwork of IA regimes and public registries across Canada that collect and share relevant documents associated with mining development. While many mines in Canada are included in a recent global database of metal and coal mines (Jasansky et al. 2023) and a database of historically producing mines in Canada (Dallaire-Fortier 2024 _a_), there is no centralized database that would allow understanding of the full scope of mines that have been assessed under IA processes in Canada. Although transparency is a cornerstone of good IA and regulatory practice (Westwood et al. 2019; Hunsberger et al. 2020) and an explicit objective of some IA and open data policies or legislation (Government of Alberta 2015; Government of Ontario 2020; Olszynski and Ray 2020; Nova Scotia Department of Environment and Climate Change 2023; Impact Assessment Agency of Canada 2024), a great deal of information remains unavailable to the public or is prohibitively difficult to access.

Our objectives are to (1) present the first complete list of all federal and provincial IA laws that currently apply or have historically applied to mining projects; (2) present a list of mines and quarries that have undergone IA under those laws in Canada and their characteristics; (3) quantify trends in mining and IA over time; and (4) assess the transparency and quality of information about mining-related IA by jurisdiction. Our summaries and raw data are available for researchers and the public in the view of further investigating mining trends in Canada.

## Materials and methods

### Generating the project list

Between August 2023 and December 2024, we searched the Canadian Legal Information Institute database (CanLII 2025) using its “document title” search function and the search terms “environmental assessment”, “impact assessment” and, if necessary, adding the name of the jurisdiction. We recorded the jurisdiction, statute name, and any ensuing regulations providing substantive guidance on IA, the year in which each law or regulation was enacted, and the link where it was available. For each jurisdiction, we briefly summarized the law or policy guidance underpinning the currently active IA process for proposed mines and quarries (Supplementary Material 1). We located each jurisdiction's IA registry by using Google's search engine and/or government websites as necessary.

Our study scope included all mines or quarry projects in Canada that had completed the IA process through any federal, provincial or territorial regime as of 31 December 2023. To allow consistency when comparing among jurisdictions, we did not include projects that were withdrawn by proponents, terminated by regulatory agencies, historically abandoned and/or closed mines that underwent an IA solely for purposes of site remediation/cleanup, IAs for mineral exploration/drilling, and projects that were “registered” for IA but screened out of the legislated process (e.g., did not meet the anticipated production threshold). To allow for direct comparisons between mineral production trends/metrics, mines and quarries that were initially constructed without having gone through an IA process (e.g., built prior to the coming-in-to-force of the IA law in that jurisdiction) were not included within our study scope, even if IA laws or regulations were used to change the project later. Only the initial IA was captured within our database for mines that underwent IA and were expanded later on, either through project amendments (see Collison et al. 2022) or subsequent IAs for major mine expansions (see Adams et al. 2025). For projects subject to federal IA laws (_CEAA 1992_ or _CEAA 2012_), we excluded those where the proponent was a “federal authority”, meaning that the project was proposed on federal lands (e.g., national parks, airports, small craft harbours, First Nations reserves) as these follow a different IA procedure.

We attempted to streamline data collection by requesting data directly from offices or departments overseeing IA in each jurisdiction. We used a standard form email to request data, including descriptive characteristics of all mines meeting our study scope in their jurisdiction. A summary of our information-gathering efforts is available in Supplementary Material 2, and redacted copies of all correspondence and data received are available [on GitHub](https://github.com/WestwoodLab/Mining-Project/tree/main/P1%3A%20Mines%2C%20mines%20and%20more%20mines)).

Although some jurisdictions provided partially complete data, none shared a comprehensive database fulfilling our request. Instead, we manually searched each jurisdiction's registry to generate a list of mines and quarries, with search procedures adapted to the constraints of each registry's portal. Many registries were incomplete and either did not include projects assessed prior to when digitized information was readily available or were missing key documents (like Environmental Impact Statements (EIS)) from listed projects. As public access to information is crucial for stakeholders and rightsholders to effectively participate in IA (Odparlik and Köppel 2013), we also assessed the functionality and level of document availability within each IA public registry.

To obtain information not available on registries or through email communications with each jurisdiction, we submitted freedom of information (FOI) requests to the provinces of Saskatchewan, Québec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick (Supplementary Material 2). New Brunswick provided us with the documents we requested within their mandated 30-day timeline. We received some of the documents requested from Saskatchewan six months after submitting the initial request. Québec took longer than the statutory response period to reply, at which time they informed us that they had no documents that met the parameters of our request. We did not proceed with our FOI request with Nova Scotia as we did not have funding for the estimated 1440 CAD search fee (adjusted from 6000 CAD after reducing the scope of our request). Although we would have included paper records had they been provided, ultimately, our final project list consisted of entirely electronic records from online registries and data provided directly by contacted jurisdictions. When a project was included in the registries of more than one jurisdiction, we captured both assessments (including harmonized, duplicated, and substituted assessments).

### Data extraction and analysis

Each project on the list was subject to data extraction by one of five reviewers. One of the study leads provided a 1 h training session on data extraction to all reviewers following a standard protocol (Supplementary Material 3). All reviewers completed an example data extraction together. Drop-in sessions were held weekly during the data extraction period for reviewers to ask questions or troubleshoot with a study lead.

To our knowledge, a universal classification scheme for materials extracted from mines and quarries does not exist. As such, materials were classed a priori using classifications from the International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM 2025) and Shanghai Metal Market (2025), adapted to a Canadian context (Table 1). During a preliminary review of IA documents from a subset of projects, we noted that some proponents used volumetric measurements commonly used in their respective industries (e.g., cubic metres of peat moss or barrels of bitumen) instead of mass measurements. We also noted that some projects reported production rates based on the processed product rather than the material extracted from the ground (e.g., uranium yellowcake (U 3 O 8) instead of “pure” uranium ore). Where possible, we standardized the units for final reporting of production size as the average tonnes of target material being produced per day of operations.

For each project, reviewers collected data for 20 variables into a spreadsheet, including three “key metrics”: production size (as measured by production or processing rate), footprint (physical space taken up by infrastructure and surface disturbance), and lifespan (timeline for construction, operation, and active closure/remediation). We also captured project location, project type (underground, open pit, mixed), target commodities, material class, design characteristics (milling, ore extraction method), IA duration (date filed for project proposal, date for project rejection or approval), law or regulations under which IA was conducted, searchability of text within the documents, and links to documents consulted. When attempts were made to locate information and it could not be found, the category was recorded as “COULD NOT LOCATE”. When unreported in the relevant IA document(s) or provided in a non-standard format (e.g., lot/concession system), coordinates (decimal degrees) were extracted from the center of the mining project using Google Maps(2023).

To validate the initial round of data extraction, a proportional random sample (∼10% of projects per jurisdiction) was selected using a bounded random number generator with project ID numbers. For the 27 projects selected for validation, a different reviewer extracted data using the same protocol (Supplementary Material 3) and was blinded from the initial data collected. We compared 15 variables for agreement between each reviewer's assessment. As some variables required unit conversion and rounding, we counted continuous data as in agreement if the second recorded number was within 5% of the first attempt. We counted dates as in agreement if they were within 1 week.

Agreement between the two reviewers’ assessments ranged from 40% to 93% per project, with an average agreement of 77% (Supplementary Material 4). We then calculated percent agreement for each variable and identified nine variables with<80% agreement (Pursuant EA law, Target commodity, Production Size, Lifespan, Footprint, Layout, IA start date, Project approved date). The project team met, and discrepancies were discussed and corrected in the original database. For the variables with<80% agreement from validation, one reviewer was assigned to review every database item for these variables and make corrections if necessary. The average number of variables that required correction, per project, in the second round of data extraction was two.

When a project was assessed under multiple jurisdictions, to allow for more consistent quantitative trend analysis, we used the key metrics data from the federal IA. Project locations were mapped using ArcGIS Pro Version 3.3.1 (ESRI 2023), apart from three mines in Manitoba with unknown locations. To compare with the total mining footprint mapped by Tang and Werner (2023), we summed the footprint of projects (where these data were available). We calculated the “completeness” of data availability for our key metrics (size, lifespan, footprint) in each jurisdiction by dividing the total number of times these metrics could be extracted by the total possible if these data were available for all projects.

We compared median assessment duration statistically between laws under which projects were assessed. Since these data were non-normally distributed and had inconsistent sample sizes, we used the non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis test to compare among the 14 laws that had a minimum of 5 projects assessed included in our database. We then did pairwise comparisons using a two-sample Wilcoxon Rank-Sum test between _CEAA 2012_ and other laws that are currently in force, as well as between newer and older laws where jurisdictions had multiple laws. The threshold of statistical significance was α=0.05. All quantitative analyses to summarize the database were completed in R Studio (R version 4.3.1) (R Core Team 2023), and data visualization was done using the _ggplot2_ package (Wickham 2011).

## Results

Our search revealed that 28 IA statutes existed across 15 jurisdictions, ranging from 1 to 4 statutes per jurisdiction (Table 2). The earliest enacted law that underpinned IAs for mining projects Canada was Manitoba's _The Clean Environment Act_, CCSM 1968, c 130 (details spelled out in a Cabinet policy beginning in 1975; Manitoba Law Reform Commission 2015), and the most recent piece of new IA legislation was the federal _Impact Assessment Act_, SC 2019, c 28. Some jurisdictions, such as the Inuvialuit Settlement Region and Prince Edward Island, did not contain any mining projects that had completed the IA process.

We analyzed 266 assessments across 13 jurisdictions under 22 different IA laws (complete database available as Supplementary Material 5 and on [GitHub](https://github.com/WestwoodLab/Mining-Project/tree/main/P1%3A%20Mines%2C%20mines%20and%20more%20mines/Information%20Requests)). Our database comprises 227 unique mines and quarries as 39 projects were assessed under more than one jurisdiction. Nearly 80% of individual IAs analyzed in our research primary fell under 11 statutes, including two federal laws (19%), two Manitoba laws (16%), two British Columbia laws (12%), two Alberta laws (10%), and individual statutes in Saskatchewan (11%), Québec (8%), and Newfoundland and Labrador (7%). Reported values for our key metrics ranged greatly on an IA-by-IA basis, with production capacities ranging from 8 to 153 200 tonnes of ore per day, lifespans ranging from 2.5 to 103.5 years, and footprints ranging from 1 to 29 217 ha.

Sixty-four percent of projects assessed under both a provincial and federal IA regime (_n_=39) showed discrepancies between the key quantitative metrics of production size, footprint, and lifespan (Table 3). Of the projects with discrepancies (_n_=25), their reported size differed the most (84% of cases), followed by lifespan (68%), and footprint (60%). For example, the Kami Iron Ore Project (assessed under _CEAA 1992_ and Newfoundland and Labrador's _EPA 2002_), ore production rates were markedly different (43 800 tonnes/day as compared to 104 000 tonnes/day), as was lifespan (18 vs. 21 years), and footprint (7625 ha federally, 2379 ha provincially). Although the Kearl Oil Sands Mine submitted a project with a smaller size to the provincial regulator (Alberta) than the federal one, perplexingly, its predicted footprint was reported as more than double to the provincial regulator. Both projects in Alberta showed discrepancies. In Québec, every project showed discrepancies, with some being very large (the size reported in provincial documents for the Akasaba West mine was triple that submitted to the federal regular, and footprint was double). The average difference in assessment start date (when the provincial vs. federal regulator received the EIA application documents) was 327 days for projects with discrepancies. The average difference in date when the IA process started for projects without discrepancies (_n_=14) was 208 days.

### Access to information

The availability of relevant IA documents and data varied significantly by jurisdiction (Table 4). British Columbia and the three territories (Yukon, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut) were the only jurisdictions with full document availability for every project beginning at the introduction of an EIA legislative framework in their respective jurisdictions. Advanced filters to narrow search criteria and built-in interactive maps with project locations aided in the navigability of these four registries for efficient data extraction. Document availability for projects that had undergone IA in the past 10–15 years was generally sufficient for most of the remaining registries, with a rapid drop-off in available information for projects assessed prior to the mid-2000s.

For the project IAs that reported production capacity (_n_=231), all metal mines (precious, ferrous, base; _n_=142) reported the metric as “ore”. Across all projects and jurisdictions, the 10 most common target commodities were gold (_n_=67), copper (_n_=32), aggregates (_n_=19), thermal coal (_n_=16), metallurgical coal (_n_=15), silver (_n_=14), zinc (_n_=14), iron (_n_=12), peat (_n_=12), and oil sands (n=11). Most projects targeted one commodity (_n_=186), 24 projects targeted two commodities, nine projects targeted three commodities, and eight projects targeted four or more commodities. Commonly co-occurring elements that were proposed to be mined together included gold and copper (_n_=16), often in conjunction with other metals like silver, zinc, lead, and/or molybdenum.

Some of the earliest IAs in our database included the Bernic Lake (Tanco) Tantalum Mine in Manitoba (1974), Nordegg Coal Mine in Alberta (1974), Bachelor Lake Gold Mine in Québec (1982), and Jolu (Mallard Lake) Gold Mine in Saskatchewan (1988). Due to difficulties accessing data prior to 1995, we only visualized trends from this year forward. Overall, production sizes and footprints of approved mines have been increasing with time. Of the 10 proposed mines rejected by their respective regulators (Fig. 4; Panel D), the smallest proposed producer was the Kiggavik Uranium Project (1000 tonnes/day) and the largest was the Kemess North Gold-Copper Mine (87 300 tonnes/day). Teck's open pit Frontier Oil Sands Mines, approved by the Government of Alberta in 2019, was by far the largest project at a proposed footprint of>29 000 ha. The second-largest project was just over half that size, also located in Alberta (Horizon Oil Sands Mine; 17 193 ha).

The trend of the late aughts continued for the 58 mines proposed from 2015 to 2023, with 55% being metal mines. Four lithium mines and two graphite mines were approved in this period—target commodities that were not present in mine IAs prior to 2015. The most recently approved major mine included in our database (November 2023) was the Rook I Uranium Project in Saskatchewan.

Overall, anticipated lifespans of proposed mines and quarries showed a great deal of variation across jurisdictions (Fig. 5; Panel A). Proposed lifespans did not differ much by mine layout or target commodity apart from a cluster of underground potash mines with long lifespans of>100 years (Fig. 5; Panel B).

### IA outcomes and timelines

Of the 227 unique projects that underwent IA between 1974 and 2023, 10 (1.8%) were rejected from provincial and/or federal IA. There were 14 total rejections, since some projects were assessed by both federal and provincial regimes. The oldest rejected project was the Whites Point Quarry in Nova Scotia (2007 assessment by review panel) and most recent was the Sukunka Coal Mine in late 2022. The remaining eight rejected mines targeted co-occurring gold and copper (_n_=5), thermal coal (_n_=1), metallurgical coal (_n_=1), or uranium (_n_=1). The Prosperity Gold-Copper Project was assessed three times and federally rejected twice (2010 and 2014), despite being approved by the British Columbia Environmental Assessment Office in 2010. The Prosperity Mine was the only example we found of IA regulators (provincial vs. federal) making a different final decision on the same project.

The amount of time it took between IA regulators receiving a project application and approving that project varied across IA jurisdictions and laws in force (Fig. 6). Average IA duration, by law, was the shortest in Nova Scotia (0.5±0.6 years), followed by Manitoba (1.2±0.8 years), Alberta's _EPEA 1992_ (1.3±0.9 years), Newfoundland and Labrador (1.7±1.8 years), British Columbia's _EAA 1996_ (2.1±1.4 years), Yukon (3.3±2.1 years), Québec (3.3±1.3 years), Alberta's _EPEA 2000_ (3.4±2.4 years), federal _CEAA 1992_ (3.5±2.3 years), Saskatchewan (3.5±2.6 years), British Columbia's _EAA 2002_ (3.7±1.9 years), Nunavut (4.4±1.0 years), federal _CEAA 2012_ (4.8±2.6 years), and Ontario (6.0±3.7 years). In all three cases where new IA legislation had been introduced (Federal, Alberta, British Columbia), the mean IA duration was slightly longer under the newer statute (Fig. 6).

Alberta's past and present laws did differ (_W_=287, _p_<0.05), with _EPEA 2000_ having significantly longer assessment durations than _EPEA 1992_.

## Discussion

We created a comprehensive list of 22 historical and current IA laws in Canada (Table 2) and a publicly available [database](https://github.com/WestwoodLab/Mining-Project/blob/52d06816a803e3ad14e9d6eaa341915514cc5ebd/P1%3A%20Mines%2C%20mines%20and%20more%20mines/Database/EIA_Mine_Database_CLEAN_duplicates_removed.xlsx) of 266 IAs for 227 mines and quarries that were assessed under these laws (Supplementary Material 5). Due to data gaps in regulator registries, the exact number of mines and quarries that underwent IA pursuant to many IA laws remains unknown. There are several projects in our database that we could confirm had undergone IA but did not have any available documents or data. Furthermore, there are projects whose existence we are unaware of because we were unable to find information that they have undergone IA (particularly those assessed prior to the early 2000s). The major themes that emerged from our analysis include difficulties accessing information, shifting trends in mining targets and regulatory regimes, and high variation in IA processes across jurisdictions. While this analysis was contained within Canada, these themes are generalizable across North America and beyond (Lamdan 2017; Ruple et al. 2022; Adams et al. 2025).

### Discoverability, access, and use of information

As evidenced by all jurisdictions having online registries, it is widely accepted in Canada that access to IA information for currently proposed projects is a public good, and important for the public and decision-makers. It is in some cases legislated for new IAs (e.g., _IAA 2019_). However, documents from past IAs are also important to ensure these groups are fully informed and that current assessments, permitting, and environmental policymaking proceeds with all the necessary context. For instance, mines often expand and change over time (Abdel Sabour and Poulin 2010; Enríquez-de-Salamanca 2016; Collison et al. 2022) and historically producing mine sites may be revitalized by mining companies (Velásquez et al. 2020; Sarker et al. 2022). These original documents can also provide important historical and baseline data to inform new assessments and regional and strategic decision-making. Where data are available, there is much research use with benefits for IA policy and practice. For example, in British Columbia, researchers have leveraged historical IA information to document overestimations of positive economic and employment impacts (Collard et al. 2023) and proponents’ tendency to submit a smaller project for IA scrutiny only to later file a less-scrutinized amendment to alter the scope of their project (Collison et al. 2022). In the latter case, the BCEAO recently updated its amendments policy to partly address this loophole (BCEAO 2024 _b_).

We experienced substantial challenges relating to IA information discoverability, access, and use. The FAIR Guiding Principles (Wilkinson et al. 2016) encourage institutions to publish findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable data. Findable data are indexed and possesses metadata that makes it easily discoverable (Wilkinson et al. 2016). Most documents generated during IA processes are meant to be available to the public to promote awareness of proposed projects (Plummer 2006), consistent with regulators maintaining public registries designed to facilitate access to these documents (Odparlik and Köppel 2013). Mining companies may also publish the relevant documents on their own platforms (Hilson 2000; Jackson et al. 2023). Few jurisdictions had readily findable data in terms of comprehensive databases that could be searched and filtered. Public IA registries in British Columbia and the three territories had a degree of completeness and useful search features that far exceeded any other jurisdiction. A lack of findability in other jurisdictions resulted in significant expenditure of effort. For example, Newfoundland and Labrador's registry could not be filtered—forcing us to review over 1300 individual projects to determine whether they met our study scope.

_Accessible_ data are open, free, and easily understood (Wilkinson et al. 2016). The four most comprehensive and navigable public registries were maintained by the Nunavut Impact Review Board (NIRB), Yukon Environmental and Socio-economic Assessment Board (YESAB), Mackenzie Valley Review Board (MVRB), and British Columbia Environmental Assessment Office (BCEAO), and all other jurisdictions were lacking to varying degrees. The federal Impact Assessment Agency of Canada (IAAC) registry had a highly navigable interface, including a new [interactive assessment map](https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/7d41cd467df547b9a4d123b1e6ea5ed7/?locale=en-ca), but simultaneously had noticeable deficits in documentation access for projects assessed prior to _CEAA 2012_. Some jurisdictions only included accessible data after a certain year (e.g., Nova Scotia) and others posed great difficulty to even understanding what was accessible (e.g., Québec, Manitoba). Manitoba and Saskatchewan's registries offered little to no documentation about the projects assessed during the first 30–35 years of their respective jurisdictions’ IA laws (before ∼2012), which made it unclear what data has been maintained over this extended period.

Our efforts to use FOI to access information not posted on public registries were largely unsuccessful due to prohibitive fees and/or timelines that extended into the years (Supplementary Material 2). Our email correspondence with regulatory agencies greatly varied in the willingness to respond, guide, and support our request, with some being particularly helpful (e.g., IAAC, Newfoundland and Labrador, the Northwest Territories) and others posing challenges and administrative roadblocks (e.g., Nova Scotia, Québec) (Supplementary Material 2).

_Interoperable_ data are formal, structured, and referenced through their metadata (Wilkinson et al. 2016). We were not surprised at a lack of interoperability between jurisdictions, as different laws and registries have different standards and data reporting requirements (Hickey et al. 2010). However, we were surprised at the lack of interoperability within jurisdictions. For example, for oil sands projects assessed in Alberta, production capacity was captured in a myriad of different ways (e.g., barrels of bitumen per day, millions of cubic metres of raw unprocessed material over the project's lifetime). Future research could examine the relationship between the terms of reference issued by jurisdictions and the interoperability of data for different project types. Another within-jurisdiction comparison that may warrant further investigation is the difference in data interoperability for mining IAs conducted under the same IA law but located in southern vs. northern (covered by the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement) Québec. Interoperable information is essential to support the analyses required for regional, strategic, and cumulative effects assessments.

Reusable data are linked to their provenance, meaning that they are richly described and meets clear data usage standards (Wilkinson et al. 2016). We did not investigate data useability, but studies that have evaluated IA data reusability related to different project aspects found substantial variation across individual projects and proponents (Anifowose et al. 2016; Cole et al. 2022; Brown et al. 2024).

### Contextualizing trends in commodities and regulation

Mining trends are governed by an intertwined set of complex forces including deposit discovery and accessibility, technology, politics, social license, legitimacy, regulation, national and international markets, foreign relations, jurisdiction, and more. Broadly speaking, when looking at mines and quarries in our Canadian database, we saw a trend of proposed oil sands and coal projects before 2010, and after this time, proposals began to shift to commodities associated with renewable energy and advanced technologies (e.g., lithium, nickel, rare earth metals). Despite the recognized need to shift to mining critical minerals (Sovacool et al. 2020), precious material (gold, silver, diamond) proposals were relatively stable over time as constantly desired target commodities. Across commodity types, proposed mines became substantially larger in terms of both production size and footprint after 2010. Although the planned footprint could only be extracted for 65% of the projects in our database, the total proposed footprint of all mines and quarries (3274 km 2) reported here closely resembles the 3319 km 2 of active mine footprint in Canada mapped by Tang and Werner (2023).

The early 1980s is when IA as a concept involving quantifiable and systematic prediction and evaluation of harms and benefits became popularized in Canada (Beanlands and Duinker 1984). Although a few IA-specific statutes were established prior to 1990s (e.g., Newfoundland and Labrador's _Environmental Assessment Act, SNL 1980, c 3_), most jurisdictions with separate IA statutes enacted them in the mid-1990s. This coincides with what Dallaire-Fortier (2025) describes as the regime of “negotiated legitimacy” in Canadian mining history, with IA as a tool for facilitating scrutiny of proposed projects by the public, Indigenous Nations, and the government. During this time, the concept of “sustainable mining” becomes part of national discourse and “impact-benefit agreements” with Indigenous Nations became commonplace associated with major projects (Dallaire-Fortier 2025).

Ostensibly, projects which are approved through IA processes have passed public and government scrutiny and might be considered “legitimized”. In our database we found that proposed projects had an extremely high IA approval rate of 96%. Similarly, of 806 proposed projects (including for developments other than mines) in Australia between 2000 and 2015, 99% were approved (Milman and Evershed 2015). It is possible that projects that would not have passed review were withdrawn at earlier stages of IA or never submitted in the first place because of economic headwinds or declining social licence (Fonseca and Gibson 2021). It is also possible that project proponents work with regulators “behind the scenes” prior to their submission get feedback on whether their proposal is likely to pass review and adjust accordingly before making formal submissions. This could be studied using FOI requests for regulators’ project records; however, given our experience with FOI processes, it may be difficult to do so unless these data access processes are improved.

A highly politicized factor in Canadian IA is the time elapsed between when a project is registered for assessment and when it is approved. Parties on the conservative end of the political spectrum argue that IA adds unnecessary red tape to slow industrial development (Ellis 2022), while parties on the left-leaning end of the political spectrum argue that IA needs to occur at a gradual enough pace to allow environmental and social impacts to be thoroughly considered (Lavoie 2018). When the federal _CEAA 2012_ was introduced, it was seen by those critical of the new law as a means to streamline the prior _CEAA 1992_ with the goal of faster assessments and drastically fewer projects included under its purview (Doelle 2012; Gibson 2012; Kirchhoff and Tsuji 2014). Although our list of mine and quarry projects assessed under _CEAA 1992_ is incomplete, for the 27 projects we included, there was no statistically significant difference in assessment length compared to the 23 projects in our database assessed under _CEAA 2012_. This may be partly explained by large variability in timelines between proposal and approval under _CEAA 2012_, ranging from 2 years (Black Point Quarry) to 13 years (Marathon Palladium Project).

Generally, the smaller projects included in our database were subject to a provincial IA, depending on the triggers and requirements in that jurisdiction (Supplementary Material 1). These projects may be less complex and require less time needed to predict and evaluate a project's impacts. Provinces like British Columbia, Alberta, and Québec with larger subsurface deposits are likely to attract larger mines (e.g., substantial oil sands and gold–copper mines) that require longer timelines needed for analysis, which may explain why they were not significantly different than federal timelines (Supplementary Material 6; Figs. S2 and S3).

We would have liked to compare to the _IAA 2019_ to other laws, but at the time of data collection, insufficient projects had completed assessment under the newer law. There has been significant federal government attention directed at reducing the time associated with environmental licensing, particularly for energy and mining projects associated with “clean growth” (Ministerial Working Group on Regulatory Efficiency for Clean Growth Projects 2024). Although they did not specifically investigate IA timelines, Collard et al. (2024) found that in British Columbia it is typically economic factors that drive post-IA delays to mine operations rather than licensing and permitting requirements. Research is needed to understand the relative contributions of regulations as contrasted with the labour force, production, and economic factors (including development costs and commodity pricing) to understand project approvals, rejections, and delays under the _IAA 2019_ and other laws.

### Moving towards a harmonized and clear IA system in Canada

Canada has a rich, albeit varied history of trying to achieve cooperation and reduce duplication of IA processes across its federal system (e.g., Kennett 1993; Fitzpatrick and Sinclair 2009; Fitzpatrick et al. 2024). Cooperation agreements were signed between seven provinces/territories and the federal government in the mid 2000s under _CEAA 1992_. Only British Columbia continued collaboration efforts with follow up agreements for IAs under _CEAA 2012_ and _IAA 2019_ (Impact Assessment Agency of Canada 2020).

The multi-jurisdictional legislative IA context in Canada resulted in some cases (15% of our database, _n_=39) where proponents set out to build one mine and triggered two simultaneous IAs. While a detailed investigation into each of these cases is outside the scope of our study, we found that these simultaneous and/or duplicated IAs showed considerable discrepancies in key metrics. British Columbia showed fewer discrepancies than other jurisdictions, potentially due to its cooperation agreements with the federal government that set the standards for IA substitution. Yet, serious misalignments remained: for example, the Prosperity Gold Mine was approved by British Columbia and rejected twice by the federal government (Mehdic et al. 2020; MacPhail et al. 2022; Wilson and Allard 2023). There were vast differences in key metrics for the eight mines assessed both in Québec and federally. Production rate for mines assessed both federally and in Québec differed by an average of 17 238 tonnes/day, over five times the baseline production capacity (3000 tonnes/day) for a large metal mine to trigger a federal IA under _CEAA 2012_.

One factor that may explain some of these cases is the differences in time at which various stages of the IA proceed—even differences of months to a single year may matter greatly. The economics of developing a large-scale mine are dynamic; over a period of days to months, production plans may change in response to economic factors like commodity pricing and geopolitics (Mishra and Mohanty 2020; Suárez Nieto et al. 2024). Meanwhile, IA might be proceeding with stakeholder and rightsholder input on an outdated project proposal. Economic feasibility studies are not explicitly mandated under most IA regimes in Canada (though proponents may elect to conduct one). Requiring economic feasibility studies before or during the IA process would help provide greater certainty and transparency around operational plans (Bullock and Mernitz 2017) which are undergoing impact predictions and community consultations.

The division of powers established in the Canadian constitution related to the environment generally (and therefore IA) has been subject to repeated attention by the Supreme Court of Canada. The most recent 2023 decision (_Reference re Impact Assessment Act, 2023 SCC 23_), reaffirmed earlier cases (_Friends of the Oldman River Society v. Canada (Minister of Transport), 1992 110 (SCC), [1992] 1 SCR 3_; _References re Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act, 2021 SCC 11, [2021] 1 SCR 175_) that found both the federal and provincial governments have jurisdiction over IA, but the application of _IAA 2019_ had, in certain areas, overstepped federal jurisdiction into provincial matters. In response to this reference case, the _IAA 2019_ was amended in 2024 to narrow its attention to effects within federal jurisdiction. In its conclusion, the SCC decision offers (paragraph 216): “it is open to Parliament and the provincial legislatures to exercise their respective powers over the environment harmoniously, in the spirit of cooperative federalism”.

We echo the spirit of this decision and encourage greater cooperation across Canada with respect to IA. Jurisdictional siloing, as framed by Johnston et al. (2025), poses challenges to best practices of IA which includes a holistic approach to cumulative effects assessment and efforts to ensure decisions are considered in the context of sustainability. Jurisdictional siloing also perpetuates uneven application of IA to proposed mines and quarries by fragmenting data records. Siloing paired with “project splitting” (when the assessing jurisdiction narrowly frames its review to separate project components; Doelle 2010; Enríquez-de-Salamanca 2016) can significantly hinder the ability for researchers and communities to compare proposed environmental and/or social impacts among and between projects. For example, the Lynn Lake Gold Project underwent duplicated IAs, both of which concluded in 2023, under the federal _CEAA 2012_ and Manitoba _EA 1988_. We could not compare the two sets of reported key project metrics between these two jurisdictions because the federal assessment examined the project in its entirety (Stantec Consulting Ltd. 2020 _a_), whereas the province split the project into two separate IAs: the Gordon pit (Stantec Consulting Ltd. 2020 _b_) and the MacLellan pit (Stantec Consulting Ltd. 2020 _c_). More attention must be paid to improving coordination and cooperation between the federal, provincial, territorial, and/or Indigenous governments engaged in IA (see Fitzpatrick et al. 2024; Johnston et al. 2025).

In 2025, international trade disputes and political shifts drew announcements from different levels of Canadian government regarding “fast-tracked” (Government of British Columbia 2025; Government of Ontario 2025), or “one-window” (Government of Canada 2025) IAs. These announcements have resulted in new laws being passed at national (_One Canadian Economy Act_, SC 2025, c 2) and subnational (_Protecting Ontario by Unleashing our Economy Act_, SO 2025, c 4; _Infrastructure Projects Act_, SBC 2025, c 13) levels, with streamlined permitting of mines—especially for critical minerals—as a common thread throughout (Deberdt and Letourneau 2025). How these laws are implemented, and if other provinces and territories follow suit with their own laws or policies to de-couple the practice of IA from mining development, remains to be seen. If jurisdictions wish to efficiently conduct mine and quarry IAs while striving for transparent and robust processes, they should follow three recommendations:

1.

Jurisdictions should clearly distinguish what types of mines (if any) are eligible for streamlined IA, and under what rationale. For example, if streamlining is geared towards the exploitation of critical minerals, regulators should outline explicit and measurable criteria for what projects this includes to avoid risking non-critical mines (e.g., gold mines that produce a small amount of copper) being lumped together with critical ones.

2.

Harmonization should be done in an _upwards_ fashion (Kwasniak 2009), meaning the more rigorous IA regime should be used if regulators truly intend to achieve the “highest standards for safety, environmental protection, and Indigenous consultation” (Government of Canada 2025). For example, IAs under Nova Scotia's _Environment Act_, SNS 1994-95, c 1 do not require cumulative effects to be considered; thus, an upwards-harmonized IA for a new mine in Nova Scotia would adopt the cumulative effects considerations (s. 22(1)) from the _IAA 2019_.

3.

Most importantly, harmonization and fast-tracking efforts need to ensure the duty to consult with Indigenous Peoples is executed fulsomely and in good faith (Booth and Skelton 2011; Craik 2015; Buchan 2019; Nishima-Miller et al. 2024), as well as meaningful public participation. This has been a barrier to past attempts to streamline IA (Mikadze 2016; Johnston 2024). For example, pipeline approvals under _CEAA 2012_ were overturned by courts on the basis of inadequate consultation of Indigenous peoples (_Gitxaala Nation v. Canada, 2016 FCA 187_; _Tsleil-Waututh Nation v. Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 153_). The recently passed streamlining laws are already receiving pushback, protests, and legal action from Indigenous groups and civil society actors (Chandler 2025; Chiefs of Ontario 2025; Jones 2025). Lessons from the near history suggest that a lack of meaningful consultation with rights-holders on new projects is likely to result in legal action that could delay project development for considerably longer than it would take to complete a rigorous project-level IA, or halt development entirely.

## Conclusion

We present a first-of-its-kind database of mines and quarries, which have undergone IA in jurisdictions across Canada. Due to the incompleteness of regulator registries, there are many data gaps in both the list of projects and the key metrics we extracted. Nevertheless, researchers can use our database to further elaborate on jurisdictional, economic, and policy trends. A particularly interesting question would be to examine the fate of these projects and audit how their built size, lifespan, and projections of economic and environmental impact aligned with what was proposed. Collard et al. (2023) have developed an IA auditing method that could be applied to our database, in combination with other datasets such as those that track mine closures (Dallaire-Fortier 2024 _b_).

Based on our findings, we have several recommendations for regulators. We encourage all jurisdictions to adopt the FAIR principles (Wilkinson et al. 2016) for data sharing of public records through both IA registries and mining recorders’ offices. Strides to increase data availability must respect the ownership, control, access, and possession (OCAP) principles and rights of Indigenous peoples who are involved with IAs or other forms of planning and decision-making processes (Eckert et al. 2020; Cannon et al. 2024; Corston et al. 2024). Regulators should, at minimum, ensure that project proponents report the key metrics of production size, footprint, and lifespan in major assessment documents (e.g., project description, EIS) with clear explanations for how these metrics are calculated. Ideally, these key metrics should be shared on registry landing pages for each project.

To support interoperability, we encourage regulators to cooperate with one another to standardize these metrics among project types. This could be accomplished by having regulators coordinate the information they request in the terms of reference that are given to project proponents at the outset of IA processes. Definitions of production size should be standardized within and between project classes (as feasible) with clearly specified units (e.g., tonnes of ore/day). Lifespan should distinguish between the proposed durations of each project phase (e.g., construction, operations, active closure, passive remediation, follow-up monitoring). At present, some projects only provide _footprint_ calculations based on major mine components (pits, processing facilities) while excluding utility/road corridors. Instead of the planned physical footprint, some proposals only reported a regional “study area” (e.g., project site+500 m buffer) and others only provided information on “disturbed habitat” for a particular species. How footprint is to be calculated should be clearly delineated in terms of reference and aligned across jurisdictions. Finally, as different levels of government continue to politicize discussions about IA timelines, jurisdictions should coordinate to standardize what event determines the “start” of an IA process. For example, in Alberta, the “start” is based on when an EIS is submitted, whereas in the federal process, the “start” begins when a (pre-EIS) project description is submitted.

To facilitate access to information, all jurisdictions’ online registries should be updated include search functions as well as the ability to filter by variables including the law under which a project was assessed, project class, target commodity, year ranges, and others. We encourage regulators to continue to make project documents accessible online, including digitizing paper records from past IAs. Some of Canada's IA agencies pride themselves on transparency and opportunities for public involvement (Gilmour and Stacey 2024), so we posit that digitizing files from historical IAs (usually already held within government purview) would be a proactive short-term minimal cost with long lasting benefits. We encountered significant roadblocks when engaging in FOI processes, and these processes have been criticized for not adequately supporting the public's right to information (Black 2023; Cardaso and Doolittle 2024; Laroche 2024). Jurisdictions should make sure their FOI processes are clear, easy to navigate, and to hold to their own prescribed timelines for responding to FOI requests.

Moving forward, legal and policy changes can support clearer and more aligned IA practices in Canada. This will become particularly important as Indigenous-led assessment becomes more common (First Nations Energy and Mining Council 2019; Bruce et al. 2024; [Nishima-Miller et al. 2024](https://www.facetsjournal.com/doi/full/10.1139/facets-2025

# Unearthing trends in environmental impact assessments for mines and quarries across Canada

## Abstract

In Canada, at least 200 active mines and 6500 quarries produce 60 commodities. Many proposed mines and quarries undergo impact assessment (IA) to predict potential impacts and inform final decision-making, alongside conditions for mitigating risk. We (1) present the first complete list of IA laws that apply to mining in Canada; (2) provide an open-source database of mine and quarry projects subject to IA; (3) quantify mining and IA trends; and (4) assess availability of information by jurisdiction. Our database includes 266 assessments of 227 projects under 13 jurisdictions proposed from 1974 to 2023. Over time, target commodities shifted from coal, oil sands, and peat, to metals (e.g., gold, copper, nickel) and production sizes increased. For many projects assessed across multiple jurisdictions, we could not explain differences in reported key metrics (production size, lifespan, footprint). Our database's comprehensiveness is limited by a lack of publicly available data. We recommend regulators adopt the findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable principles for information sharing by standardizing key metrics, publishing project documentation, and improving registry functionality. We encourage enhanced inter-jurisdictional IA cooperation to ensure the public and decision-makers have access to fulsome information about new projects during a modern mineral rush in Canada.

## Introduction

With increased global population and resource use, mining pressures are accelerating (Heffron 2020), and rates of metal extraction are expected to increase (Schandl et al. 2020). Mineral development trends are changing in response to a desire to exploit “critical minerals”, including those argued as necessary for green technologies and renewable infrastructure (Deetman et al. 2018; Sovacool et al. 2020). In Canada, this has been evidenced by the launch of the 4 billion CAD Canadian Critical Minerals Strategy (Natural Resources Canada 2022), intended to accelerate production and recycling of critical minerals while meeting social and environmental goals.

Since European colonization, mineral extraction has been an important part of the Canadian economy (McNeill and Vrtis 2017; Sandlos and Keeling 2021). The first “industrial-scale” mines were built in the 1730s through the 1890s, extracting iron and coal in Québec and Nova Scotia, respectively (Millward 1984; Samson 1998). Precious metal discoveries also spurred treaty-making between settlers and First Nations in Northern Ontario in the 1840s (Morrison 1986). In 2021, over 200 mines and 6500 quarries produced 60 minerals and metals used in goods worldwide, a sector comprising 6% of Canada's economy (Natural Resources Canada 2023). Mines in Canada occupy a surface footprint of at least 3300 km 2 (Tang and Werner 2023) and many jurisdictions in Canada are experiencing a modern-day mineral rush (Ralph et al. 2023).

### The potential consequences of increased mining pressure

Concerns have been raised about the potential risks associated with environmental regulation lagging behind the surge in development accompanying forecasted demands for critical minerals and current high prices of precious metals (Luckeneder et al. 2021; Yin et al. 2021; Kerr 2023). With public investments and commitments to “increase the supply of responsibly sourced critical minerals” (Natural Resources Canada 2022) and “protect 25% of Canada's marine and terrestrial area by 2025 and … 30% by 2030” (Environment and Climate Change Canada 2023) government agencies across Canada are attempting to strike a delicate balance between growing the mineral sector and delivering on conservation targets.

The exact number of abandoned mines (sites that have been left without proper rehabilitation) across the country remains unknown. Conservative estimates suggest that there are over 10 000 such sites (Mackasey 2000; Natural Resources Canada 2010; Tremblay and Hogan 2016), many of which continue to pollute the environment decades to centuries after ceasing operations (Keeling 2010; Sandlos and Keeling 2016; Cooke et al. 2024). Advancements in remote sensing technology and climate-driven reductions in permafrost, glacier, and sea ice area may increase access to remote areas for mineral exploration (Plante et al. 2018; Walter et al. 2020; Shirmard et al. 2022; Moore et al. 2023) and potentially result in wider anthropogenic impacts across Canada (Austin et al. 2025). Cumulative effects of industrial activities on communities and the environment have been poorly managed to date (Duinker and Greig 2006; Atlin and Gibson 2017). Aquatic ecosystems remain particularly vulnerable to cumulative effects of historical, operating, and future mining developments (Sergeant et al. 2022; Simpson and Collison 2022). Ecologically significant habitat for sensitive species, such as caribou and salmon, remain at high risk for future mining pressure (Collard et al. 2020; Sergeant et al. 2022).

Well-publicized examples of major impacts on environmental and human health include the consequences of mountaintop removal coal mining in British Columbia's Elk Valley and the Mount Polley tailings dam failure. In the Elk Valley, high concentrations of selenium and other potentially toxic elements (Petryshen 2023; Teck Coal Limited 2023) have led to charges against mine proponents for polluting fish-bearing waterways (Cruickshank 2024) and contributed to Canada–US political tensions (Cruickshank 2023). The Mount Polley tailings dam failure was the world's second-largest such catastrophe, and severely impacted aquatic life and Indigenous communities downstream (Shandro et al. 2017; Byrne et al. 2018). Another recent disaster that continues to unfold is the heap leach pad failure at the Eagle Gold Mine in the Yukon, with the long-term environmental damage largely unknown (Elliot 2025; Government of Yukon 2025). Beyond these examples, ongoing chemical contamination from mine tailings in Canada has been documented from 10 to over 100 years post-mine closure in variety of environments, with impacts on biological communities in freshwater systems throughout (Dickman 1991; Maqsoud et al. 2016; Sprague and Vermaire 2018; Little et al. 2020; Perrett et al. 2021; Jacques and Pienitz 2022).

### Regulation of mining development in Canada

Canada is one of 25 federalist countries in the world (Loomis et al. 2021), which assigns jurisdiction to either the national (i.e., federal) or sub-national (i.e., provincial) government through s. 91 and 92 of the _Constitution Act 1867_, 30 & 31 Vict, c 3. Regulation of “the environment”, including impact assessment (IA), is not assigned in the Constitution; the courts have decided that both levels of government have obligations in this area, leading to overlapping and messy legislative responsibilities (Valiante 2002; Fitzpatrick et al. 2021). The consequence of this distribution of powers is that mining regulation is materially different depending on where it takes place in Canada. Generally, the federal government cannot exercise powers in areas under provincial jurisdiction (except in instances of true conflict between federal and provincial laws). With regard to mining, provincial governments have exclusive jurisdiction related to the exploration, development, and management of non-renewable resources within their territories. Uranium is an exception to this rule—the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission regulates uranium mines and milling facilities in addition to oversight from the provinces on uranium exploration and compliance monitoring of operations (Natural Resources Canada 2024). While territorial governments do not have powers assigned by the Constitution, the federal government has devolved many of the powers associated with mineral development to Yukon and Northwest Territories, with devolution to Nunavut continuing into 2027. In other words, regulation of mining is primarily the responsibility of each province and territory.1

The process of proposing a new mine begins with a mining claim made in that jurisdiction. At present, most subsurface claims are established through the “free entry” principle, whereby in most provincial and territorial jurisdictions in Canada, any person with a mineral prospecting licence (which requires no special certifications) pays a small fee to stake a claim on subsurface rights to an area. The free entry process has been heavily criticized (Hoogeveen 2015; Tollefson 2021) and may change soon because of court challenges proceeding in several jurisdictions2 British Columbia recently introduced First Nations’ consultation requirements for mineral claim staking, in response to legal action from the Gitxaala Nation (British Columbia Ministry of Mining and Critical Minerals 2025). Some industry groups have claimed that new consultation rules will create instability in mineral exploration investment (Association for Mineral Exploration 2025), whereas the regional chief of the BC Assembly of First Nations was critical that the new requirements did not go far enough, stating that it “risks perpetuating business-as-usual practices that exclude First Nations from critical decision-making processes” (Teegee 2025). To move forward from mining claims and exploration towards construction and operation of a mine, proponents are required to receive several approvals, which vary by jurisdiction, type of mine, and size of mine.

Canadian provinces began introducing IA policies in the early 1970s, which were initially largely voluntary and non-binding. Ontario was the first province to enact legislation in this regard in 1975 (_The Environmental Assessment Act_, SO 1975, c 69), with other jurisdictions doing so in the following decades. Since the 1980s, legislation and policies based on the practice of IA have been used to assess a proposed mine's environmental, economic, and social effects prior to approvals and authorizations. At the level of an individual project, IA processes are used to inform decision-makers on whether to approve the project (and if so, with what conditions), and proponents are either mandated or encouraged to seek input from the public and Indigenous rights-holders (Stewart and Sinclair 2007). There are also other forms of IA besides that for individual projects, such as strategic environmental assessment, sustainability assessment, cumulative effects assessment, life-cycle assessment, social impact assessment, and health impact assessment, among others (e.g., Fitzpatrick and Sinclair 2009; Morgan 2012; Retief et al. 2014; Bond 2015; Johnson 2015).

Although project-level IA typically follows a similar process (e.g., establish the scope of the assessment, identify potential impacts, mitigate negative impacts, determine residual effects, and make a decision if the project should proceed), there are significant procedural variations across time and space (Gibson 2002; Hickey et al. 2010; Fitzpatrick et al. 2021). In different jurisdictions and under different laws, IAs have differing scope (i.e., factors that must be considered in the assessment), requirements or opportunities for public participation, and requirements for consultation of Indigenous peoples, among other provisions (see Supplementary Material 1 for an explanation of how IA applies to mines in each jurisdiction).

Importantly, each jurisdiction has a set of “triggers” that determine which kinds of mines and quarries are subject to IA, and these triggers are generally related to production size, target commodity, jurisdictional powers, and other factors. Some projects may be assessed under more than one jurisdiction: for example, the largest metal mines (production size≥5000 tonnes ore/day) that are deemed as having the potential to cause impacts within federal jurisdiction (e.g., fisheries, migratory birds, Indigenous peoples’ rights and well-being) are subject to a federal IA, often in addition to a provincial IA (Johnston et al. 2025). For projects that are required to undergo IA and subsequently receive approval, proponents usually must proceed through other authorizations and permitting processes (e.g., _Fisheries Act_ authorizations or converting exploration licenses into mining leases) before construction can begin. In addition, regulatory requirements continue to apply throughout the operations, closure, and post-closure phases of the project. While the foundational principles of IA have been respected in law for decades in Canada, its dubious future implementation is a result of government and industry criticism against IA for hindering economic development, including the exploitation of critical minerals (Johnston 2024; Wright and Olszynski 2025).

### Objectives

There is a patchwork of IA regimes and public registries across Canada that collect and share relevant documents associated with mining development. While many mines in Canada are included in a recent global database of metal and coal mines (Jasansky et al. 2023) and a database of historically producing mines in Canada (Dallaire-Fortier 2024 _a_), there is no centralized database that would allow understanding of the full scope of mines that have been assessed under IA processes in Canada. Although transparency is a cornerstone of good IA and regulatory practice (Westwood et al. 2019; Hunsberger et al. 2020) and an explicit objective of some IA and open data policies or legislation (Government of Alberta 2015; Government of Ontario 2020; Olszynski and Ray 2020; Nova Scotia Department of Environment and Climate Change 2023; Impact Assessment Agency of Canada 2024), a great deal of information remains unavailable to the public or is prohibitively difficult to access.

Our objectives are to (1) present the first complete list of all federal and provincial IA laws that currently apply or have historically applied to mining projects; (2) present a list of mines and quarries that have undergone IA under those laws in Canada and their characteristics; (3) quantify trends in mining and IA over time; and (4) assess the transparency and quality of information about mining-related IA by jurisdiction. Our summaries and raw data are available for researchers and the public in the view of further investigating mining trends in Canada.

## Materials and methods

### Generating the project list

Between August 2023 and December 2024, we searched the Canadian Legal Information Institute database (CanLII 2025) using its “document title” search function and the search terms “environmental assessment”, “impact assessment” and, if necessary, adding the name of the jurisdiction. We recorded the jurisdiction, statute name, and any ensuing regulations providing substantive guidance on IA, the year in which each law or regulation was enacted, and the link where it was available. For each jurisdiction, we briefly summarized the law or policy guidance underpinning the currently active IA process for proposed mines and quarries (Supplementary Material 1). We located each jurisdiction's IA registry by using Google's search engine and/or government websites as necessary.

Our study scope included all mines or quarry projects in Canada that had completed the IA process through any federal, provincial or territorial regime as of 31 December 2023. To allow consistency when comparing among jurisdictions, we did not include projects that were withdrawn by proponents, terminated by regulatory agencies, historically abandoned and/or closed mines that underwent an IA solely for purposes of site remediation/cleanup, IAs for mineral exploration/drilling, and projects that were “registered” for IA but screened out of the legislated process (e.g., did not meet the anticipated production threshold). To allow for direct comparisons between mineral production trends/metrics, mines and quarries that were initially constructed without having gone through an IA process (e.g., built prior to the coming-in-to-force of the IA law in that jurisdiction) were not included within our study scope, even if IA laws or regulations were used to change the project later. Only the initial IA was captured within our database for mines that underwent IA and were expanded later on, either through project amendments (see Collison et al. 2022) or subsequent IAs for major mine expansions (see Adams et al. 2025). For projects subject to federal IA laws (_CEAA 1992_ or _CEAA 2012_), we excluded those where the proponent was a “federal authority”, meaning that the project was proposed on federal lands (e.g., national parks, airports, small craft harbours, First Nations reserves) as these follow a different IA procedure.

We attempted to streamline data collection by requesting data directly from offices or departments overseeing IA in each jurisdiction. We used a standard form email to request data, including descriptive characteristics of all mines meeting our study scope in their jurisdiction. A summary of our information-gathering efforts is available in Supplementary Material 2, and redacted copies of all correspondence and data received are available [on GitHub](https://github.com/WestwoodLab/Mining-Project/tree/main/P1%3A%20Mines%2C%20mines%20and%20more%20mines)).

Although some jurisdictions provided partially complete data, none shared a comprehensive database fulfilling our request. Instead, we manually searched each jurisdiction's registry to generate a list of mines and quarries, with search procedures adapted to the constraints of each registry's portal. Many registries were incomplete and either did not include projects assessed prior to when digitized information was readily available or were missing key documents (like Environmental Impact Statements (EIS)) from listed projects. As public access to information is crucial for stakeholders and rightsholders to effectively participate in IA (Odparlik and Köppel 2013), we also assessed the functionality and level of document availability within each IA public registry.

To obtain information not available on registries or through email communications with each jurisdiction, we submitted freedom of information (FOI) requests to the provinces of Saskatchewan, Québec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick (Supplementary Material 2). New Brunswick provided us with the documents we requested within their mandated 30-day timeline. We received some of the documents requested from Saskatchewan six months after submitting the initial request. Québec took longer than the statutory response period to reply, at which time they informed us that they had no documents that met the parameters of our request. We did not proceed with our FOI request with Nova Scotia as we did not have funding for the estimated 1440 CAD search fee (adjusted from 6000 CAD after reducing the scope of our request). Although we would have included paper records had they been provided, ultimately, our final project list consisted of entirely electronic records from online registries and data provided directly by contacted jurisdictions. When a project was included in the registries of more than one jurisdiction, we captured both assessments (including harmonized, duplicated, and substituted assessments).

### Data extraction and analysis

Each project on the list was subject to data extraction by one of five reviewers. One of the study leads provided a 1 h training session on data extraction to all reviewers following a standard protocol (Supplementary Material 3). All reviewers completed an example data extraction together. Drop-in sessions were held weekly during the data extraction period for reviewers to ask questions or troubleshoot with a study lead.

To our knowledge, a universal classification scheme for materials extracted from mines and quarries does not exist. As such, materials were classed a priori using classifications from the International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM 2025) and Shanghai Metal Market (2025), adapted to a Canadian context (Table 1). During a preliminary review of IA documents from a subset of projects, we noted that some proponents used volumetric measurements commonly used in their respective industries (e.g., cubic metres of peat moss or barrels of bitumen) instead of mass measurements. We also noted that some projects reported production rates based on the processed product rather than the material extracted from the ground (e.g., uranium yellowcake (U 3 O 8) instead of “pure” uranium ore). Where possible, we standardized the units for final reporting of production size as the average tonnes of target material being produced per day of operations.

For each project, reviewers collected data for 20 variables into a spreadsheet, including three “key metrics”: production size (as measured by production or processing rate), footprint (physical space taken up by infrastructure and surface disturbance), and lifespan (timeline for construction, operation, and active closure/remediation). We also captured project location, project type (underground, open pit, mixed), target commodities, material class, design characteristics (milling, ore extraction method), IA duration (date filed for project proposal, date for project rejection or approval), law or regulations under which IA was conducted, searchability of text within the documents, and links to documents consulted. When attempts were made to locate information and it could not be found, the category was recorded as “COULD NOT LOCATE”. When unreported in the relevant IA document(s) or provided in a non-standard format (e.g., lot/concession system), coordinates (decimal degrees) were extracted from the center of the mining project using Google Maps(2023).

To validate the initial round of data extraction, a proportional random sample (∼10% of projects per jurisdiction) was selected using a bounded random number generator with project ID numbers. For the 27 projects selected for validation, a different reviewer extracted data using the same protocol (Supplementary Material 3) and was blinded from the initial data collected. We compared 15 variables for agreement between each reviewer's assessment. As some variables required unit conversion and rounding, we counted continuous data as in agreement if the second recorded number was within 5% of the first attempt. We counted dates as in agreement if they were within 1 week.

Agreement between the two reviewers’ assessments ranged from 40% to 93% per project, with an average agreement of 77% (Supplementary Material 4). We then calculated percent agreement for each variable and identified nine variables with<80% agreement (Pursuant EA law, Target commodity, Production Size, Lifespan, Footprint, Layout, IA start date, Project approved date). The project team met, and discrepancies were discussed and corrected in the original database. For the variables with<80% agreement from validation, one reviewer was assigned to review every database item for these variables and make corrections if necessary. The average number of variables that required correction, per project, in the second round of data extraction was two.

When a project was assessed under multiple jurisdictions, to allow for more consistent quantitative trend analysis, we used the key metrics data from the federal IA. Project locations were mapped using ArcGIS Pro Version 3.3.1 (ESRI 2023), apart from three mines in Manitoba with unknown locations. To compare with the total mining footprint mapped by Tang and Werner (2023), we summed the footprint of projects (where these data were available). We calculated the “completeness” of data availability for our key metrics (size, lifespan, footprint) in each jurisdiction by dividing the total number of times these metrics could be extracted by the total possible if these data were available for all projects.

We compared median assessment duration statistically between laws under which projects were assessed. Since these data were non-normally distributed and had inconsistent sample sizes, we used the non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis test to compare among the 14 laws that had a minimum of 5 projects assessed included in our database. We then did pairwise comparisons using a two-sample Wilcoxon Rank-Sum test between _CEAA 2012_ and other laws that are currently in force, as well as between newer and older laws where jurisdictions had multiple laws. The threshold of statistical significance was α=0.05. All quantitative analyses to summarize the database were completed in R Studio (R version 4.3.1) (R Core Team 2023), and data visualization was done using the _ggplot2_ package (Wickham 2011).

## Results

Our search revealed that 28 IA statutes existed across 15 jurisdictions, ranging from 1 to 4 statutes per jurisdiction (Table 2). The earliest enacted law that underpinned IAs for mining projects Canada was Manitoba's _The Clean Environment Act_, CCSM 1968, c 130 (details spelled out in a Cabinet policy beginning in 1975; Manitoba Law Reform Commission 2015), and the most recent piece of new IA legislation was the federal _Impact Assessment Act_, SC 2019, c 28. Some jurisdictions, such as the Inuvialuit Settlement Region and Prince Edward Island, did not contain any mining projects that had completed the IA process.

We analyzed 266 assessments across 13 jurisdictions under 22 different IA laws (complete database available as Supplementary Material 5 and on [GitHub](https://github.com/WestwoodLab/Mining-Project/tree/main/P1%3A%20Mines%2C%20mines%20and%20more%20mines/Information%20Requests)). Our database comprises 227 unique mines and quarries as 39 projects were assessed under more than one jurisdiction. Nearly 80% of individual IAs analyzed in our research primary fell under 11 statutes, including two federal laws (19%), two Manitoba laws (16%), two British Columbia laws (12%), two Alberta laws (10%), and individual statutes in Saskatchewan (11%), Québec (8%), and Newfoundland and Labrador (7%). Reported values for our key metrics ranged greatly on an IA-by-IA basis, with production capacities ranging from 8 to 153 200 tonnes of ore per day, lifespans ranging from 2.5 to 103.5 years, and footprints ranging from 1 to 29 217 ha.

Sixty-four percent of projects assessed under both a provincial and federal IA regime (_n_=39) showed discrepancies between the key quantitative metrics of production size, footprint, and lifespan (Table 3). Of the projects with discrepancies (_n_=25), their reported size differed the most (84% of cases), followed by lifespan (68%), and footprint (60%). For example, the Kami Iron Ore Project (assessed under _CEAA 1992_ and Newfoundland and Labrador's _EPA 2002_), ore production rates were markedly different (43 800 tonnes/day as compared to 104 000 tonnes/day), as was lifespan (18 vs. 21 years), and footprint (7625 ha federally, 2379 ha provincially). Although the Kearl Oil Sands Mine submitted a project with a smaller size to the provincial regulator (Alberta) than the federal one, perplexingly, its predicted footprint was reported as more than double to the provincial regulator. Both projects in Alberta showed discrepancies. In Québec, every project showed discrepancies, with some being very large (the size reported in provincial documents for the Akasaba West mine was triple that submitted to the federal regular, and footprint was double). The average difference in assessment start date (when the provincial vs. federal regulator received the EIA application documents) was 327 days for projects with discrepancies. The average difference in date when the IA process started for projects without discrepancies (_n_=14) was 208 days.

### Access to information

The availability of relevant IA documents and data varied significantly by jurisdiction (Table 4). British Columbia and the three territories (Yukon, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut) were the only jurisdictions with full document availability for every project beginning at the introduction of an EIA legislative framework in their respective jurisdictions. Advanced filters to narrow search criteria and built-in interactive maps with project locations aided in the navigability of these four registries for efficient data extraction. Document availability for projects that had undergone IA in the past 10–15 years was generally sufficient for most of the remaining registries, with a rapid drop-off in available information for projects assessed prior to the mid-2000s.

For the project IAs that reported production capacity (_n_=231), all metal mines (precious, ferrous, base; _n_=142) reported the metric as “ore”. Quarries (_n_=26) typically reported raw aggregate volume (73%), refined silica or gypsum ore (15%), or raw peat (12%).

Across all projects and jurisdictions, the 10 most common target commodities were gold (_n_=67), copper (_n_=32), aggregates (_n_=19), thermal coal (_n_=16), metallurgical coal (_n_=15), silver (_n_=14), zinc (_n_=14), iron (_n_=12), peat (_n_=12), and oil sands (n=11). Most projects targeted one commodity (_n_=186), 24 projects targeted two commodities, nine projects targeted three commodities, and eight projects targeted four or more commodities. Commonly co-occurring elements that were proposed to be mined together included gold and copper (_n_=16), often in conjunction with other metals like silver, zinc, lead, and/or molybdenum.

Some of the earliest IAs in our database included the Bernic Lake (Tanco) Tantalum Mine in Manitoba (1974), Nordegg Coal Mine in Alberta (1974), Bachelor Lake Gold Mine in Québec (1982), and Jolu (Mallard Lake) Gold Mine in Saskatchewan (1988). Due to difficulties accessing data prior to 1995, we only visualized trends from this year forward. Overall, production sizes and footprints of approved mines have been increasing with time. Of the 10 proposed mines rejected by their respective regulators (Fig. 4; Panel D), the smallest proposed producer was the Kiggavik Uranium Project (1000 tonnes/day) and the largest was the Kemess North Gold-Copper Mine (87 300 tonnes/day). Teck's open pit Frontier Oil Sands Mines, approved by the Government of Alberta in 2019, was by far the largest project at a proposed footprint of>29 000 ha. The second-largest project was just over half that size, also located in Alberta (Horizon Oil Sands Mine; 17 193 ha).

The trend of the late aughts continued for the 58 mines proposed from 2015 to 2023, with 55% being metal mines. Four lithium mines and two graphite mines were approved in this period—target commodities that were not present in mine IAs prior to 2015. The most recently approved major mine included in our database (November 2023) was the Rook I Uranium Project in Saskatchewan.

Overall, anticipated lifespans of proposed mines and quarries showed a great deal of variation across jurisdictions (Fig. 5; Panel A). Proposed lifespans did not differ much by mine layout or target commodity apart from a cluster of underground potash mines with long lifespans of>100 years (Fig. 5; Panel B).

### IA outcomes and timelines

Of the 227 unique projects that underwent IA between 1974 and 2023, 10 (1.8%) were rejected from provincial and/or federal IA. There were 14 total rejections, since some projects were assessed by both federal and provincial regimes. The oldest rejected project was the Whites Point Quarry in Nova Scotia (2007 assessment by review panel) and most recent was the Sukunka Coal Mine in late 2022. The remaining eight rejected mines targeted co-occurring gold and copper (_n_=5), thermal coal (_n_=1), metallurgical coal (_n_=1), or uranium (_n_=1). The Prosperity Gold-Copper Project was assessed three times and federally rejected twice (2010 and 2014), despite being approved by the British Columbia Environmental Assessment Office in 2010. The Prosperity Mine was the only example we found of IA regulators (provincial vs. federal) making a different final decision on the same project.

The amount of time it took between IA regulators receiving a project application and approving that project varied across IA jurisdictions and laws in force (Fig. 6). Average IA duration, by law, was the shortest in Nova Scotia (0.5±0.6 years), followed by Manitoba (1.2±0.8 years), Alberta's _EPEA 1992_ (1.3±0.9 years), Newfoundland and Labrador (1.7±1.8 years), British Columbia's _EAA 1996_ (2.1±1.4 years), Yukon (3.3±2.1 years), Québec (3.3±1.3 years), Alberta's _EPEA 2000_ (3.4±2.4 years), federal _CEAA 1992_ (3.5±2.3 years), Saskatchewan (3.5±2.6 years), British Columbia's _EAA 2002_ (3.7±1.9 years), Nunavut (4.4±1.0 years), federal _CEAA 2012_ (4.8±2.6 years), and Ontario (6.0±3.7 years). In all three cases where new IA legislation had been introduced (Federal, Alberta, British Columbia), the mean IA duration was slightly longer under the newer statute (Fig. 6).
