Alberta's past and present laws did differ (_W_=287, _p_<0.05), with _EPEA 2000_ having significantly longer assessment durations than _EPEA 1992_.

## Discussion

We created a comprehensive list of 22 historical and current IA laws in Canada (Table 2) and a publicly available [database](https://github.com/WestwoodLab/Mining-Project/blob/52d06816a803e3ad14e9d6eaa341915514cc5ebd/P1%3A%20Mines%2C%20mines%20and%20more%20mines/Database/EIA_Mine_Database_CLEAN_duplicates_removed.xlsx) of 266 IAs for 227 mines and quarries that were assessed under these laws (Supplementary Material 5). Due to data gaps in regulator registries, the exact number of mines and quarries that underwent IA pursuant to many IA laws remains unknown. There are several projects in our database that we could confirm had undergone IA but did not have any available documents or data. Furthermore, there are projects whose existence we are unaware of because we were unable to find information that they have undergone IA (particularly those assessed prior to the early 2000s). The major themes that emerged from our analysis include difficulties accessing information, shifting trends in mining targets and regulatory regimes, and high variation in IA processes across jurisdictions. While this analysis was contained within Canada, these themes are generalizable across North America and beyond (Lamdan 2017; Ruple et al. 2022; Adams et al. 2025).

### Discoverability, access, and use of information

As evidenced by all jurisdictions having online registries, it is widely accepted in Canada that access to IA information for currently proposed projects is a public good, and important for the public and decision-makers. It is in some cases legislated for new IAs (e.g., _IAA 2019_). However, documents from past IAs are also important to ensure these groups are fully informed and that current assessments, permitting, and environmental policymaking proceeds with all the necessary context. For instance, mines often expand and change over time (Abdel Sabour and Poulin 2010; Enríquez-de-Salamanca 2016; Collison et al. 2022) and historically producing mine sites may be revitalized by mining companies (Velásquez et al. 2020; Sarker et al. 2022). These original documents can also provide important historical and baseline data to inform new assessments and regional and strategic decision-making. Where data are available, there is much research use with benefits for IA policy and practice. For example, in British Columbia, researchers have leveraged historical IA information to document overestimations of positive economic and employment impacts (Collard et al. 2023) and proponents’ tendency to submit a smaller project for IA scrutiny only to later file a less-scrutinized amendment to alter the scope of their project (Collison et al. 2022). In the latter case, the BCEAO recently updated its amendments policy to partly address this loophole (BCEAO 2024 _b_).

We experienced substantial challenges relating to IA information discoverability, access, and use. The FAIR Guiding Principles (Wilkinson et al. 2016) encourage institutions to publish findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable data. Findable data are indexed and possesses metadata that makes it easily discoverable (Wilkinson et al. 2016). Most documents generated during IA processes are meant to be available to the public to promote awareness of proposed projects (Plummer 2006), consistent with regulators maintaining public registries designed to facilitate access to these documents (Odparlik and Köppel 2013). Mining companies may also publish the relevant documents on their own platforms (Hilson 2000; Jackson et al. 2023). Few jurisdictions had readily findable data in terms of comprehensive databases that could be searched and filtered. Public IA registries in British Columbia and the three territories had a degree of completeness and useful search features that far exceeded any other jurisdiction. A lack of findability in other jurisdictions resulted in significant expenditure of effort. For example, Newfoundland and Labrador's registry could not be filtered—forcing us to review over 1300 individual projects to determine whether they met our study scope.

_Accessible_ data are open, free, and easily understood (Wilkinson et al. 2016). The four most comprehensive and navigable public registries were maintained by the Nunavut Impact Review Board (NIRB), Yukon Environmental and Socio-economic Assessment Board (YESAB), Mackenzie Valley Review Board (MVRB), and British Columbia Environmental Assessment Office (BCEAO), and all other jurisdictions were lacking to varying degrees. The federal Impact Assessment Agency of Canada (IAAC) registry had a highly navigable interface, including a new [interactive assessment map](https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/7d41cd467df547b9a4d123b1e6ea5ed7/?locale=en-ca), but simultaneously had noticeable deficits in documentation access for projects assessed prior to _CEAA 2012_. Some jurisdictions only included accessible data after a certain year (e.g., Nova Scotia) and others posed great difficulty to even understanding what was accessible (e.g., Québec, Manitoba). Manitoba and Saskatchewan's registries offered little to no documentation about the projects assessed during the first 30–35 years of their respective jurisdictions’ IA laws (before ∼2012), which made it unclear what data has been maintained over this extended period.

Our efforts to use FOI to access information not posted on public registries were largely unsuccessful due to prohibitive fees and/or timelines that extended into the years (Supplementary Material 2). Our email correspondence with regulatory agencies greatly varied in the willingness to respond, guide, and support our request, with some being particularly helpful (e.g., IAAC, Newfoundland and Labrador, the Northwest Territories) and others posing challenges and administrative roadblocks (e.g., Nova Scotia, Québec) (Supplementary Material 2).

_Interoperable_ data are formal, structured, and referenced through their metadata (Wilkinson et al. 2016). We were not surprised at a lack of interoperability between jurisdictions, as different laws and registries have different standards and data reporting requirements (Hickey et al. 2010). However, we were surprised at the lack of interoperability within jurisdictions. For example, for oil sands projects assessed in Alberta, production capacity was captured in a myriad of different ways (e.g., barrels of bitumen per day, millions of cubic metres of raw unprocessed material over the project's lifetime). Future research could examine the relationship between the terms of reference issued by jurisdictions and the interoperability of data for different project types. Another within-jurisdiction comparison that may warrant further investigation is the difference in data interoperability for mining IAs conducted under the same IA law but located in southern vs. northern (covered by the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement) Québec. Interoperable information is essential to support the analyses required for regional, strategic, and cumulative effects assessments.

Reusable data are linked to their provenance, meaning that they are richly described and meets clear data usage standards (Wilkinson et al. 2016). We did not investigate data useability, but studies that have evaluated IA data reusability related to different project aspects found substantial variation across individual projects and proponents (Anifowose et al. 2016; Cole et al. 2022; Brown et al. 2024).

### Contextualizing trends in commodities and regulation

Mining trends are governed by an intertwined set of complex forces including deposit discovery and accessibility, technology, politics, social license, legitimacy, regulation, national and international markets, foreign relations, jurisdiction, and more. Broadly speaking, when looking at mines and quarries in our Canadian database, we saw a trend of proposed oil sands and coal projects before 2010, and after this time, proposals began to shift to commodities associated with renewable energy and advanced technologies (e.g., lithium, nickel, rare earth metals). Despite the recognized need to shift to mining critical minerals (Sovacool et al. 2020), precious material (gold, silver, diamond) proposals were relatively stable over time as constantly desired target commodities. Across commodity types, proposed mines became substantially larger in terms of both production size and footprint after 2010. Although the planned footprint could only be extracted for 65% of the projects in our database, the total proposed footprint of all mines and quarries (3274 km 2) reported here closely resembles the 3319 km 2 of active mine footprint in Canada mapped by Tang and Werner (2023).

The early 1980s is when IA as a concept involving quantifiable and systematic prediction and evaluation of harms and benefits became popularized in Canada (Beanlands and Duinker 1984). Although a few IA-specific statutes were established prior to 1990s (e.g., Newfoundland and Labrador's _Environmental Assessment Act, SNL 1980, c 3_), most jurisdictions with separate IA statutes enacted them in the mid-1990s. This coincides with what Dallaire-Fortier (2025) describes as the regime of “negotiated legitimacy” in Canadian mining history, with IA as a tool for facilitating scrutiny of proposed projects by the public, Indigenous Nations, and the government. During this time, the concept of “sustainable mining” becomes part of national discourse and “impact-benefit agreements” with Indigenous Nations became commonplace associated with major projects (Dallaire-Fortier 2025).

Ostensibly, projects which are approved through IA processes have passed public and government scrutiny and might be considered “legitimized”. In our database we found that proposed projects had an extremely high IA approval rate of 96%. Similarly, of 806 proposed projects (including for developments other than mines) in Australia between 2000 and 2015, 99% were approved (Milman and Evershed 2015). It is possible that projects that would not have passed review were withdrawn at earlier stages of IA or never submitted in the first place because of economic headwinds or declining social licence (Fonseca and Gibson 2021). It is also possible that project proponents work with regulators “behind the scenes” prior to their submission get feedback on whether their proposal is likely to pass review and adjust accordingly before making formal submissions. This could be studied using FOI requests for regulators’ project records; however, given our experience with FOI processes, it may be difficult to do so unless these data access processes are improved.

A highly politicized factor in Canadian IA is the time elapsed between when a project is registered for assessment and when it is approved. Parties on the conservative end of the political spectrum argue that IA adds unnecessary red tape to slow industrial development (Ellis 2022), while parties on the left-leaning end of the political spectrum argue that IA needs to occur at a gradual enough pace to allow environmental and social impacts to be thoroughly considered (Lavoie 2018). When the federal _CEAA 2012_ was introduced, it was seen by those critical of the new law as a means to streamline the prior _CEAA 1992_ with the goal of faster assessments and drastically fewer projects included under its purview (Doelle 2012; Gibson 2012; Kirchhoff and Tsuji 2014). Although our list of mine and quarry projects assessed under _CEAA 1992_ is incomplete, for the 27 projects we included, there was no statistically significant difference in assessment length compared to the 23 projects in our database assessed under _CEAA 2012_. This may be partly explained by large variability in timelines between proposal and approval under _CEAA 2012_, ranging from 2 years (Black Point Quarry) to 13 years (Marathon Palladium Project).

Generally, the smaller projects included in our database were subject to a provincial IA, depending on the triggers and requirements in that jurisdiction (Supplementary Material 1). These projects may be less complex and require less time needed to predict and evaluate a project's impacts. Provinces like British Columbia, Alberta, and Québec with larger subsurface deposits are likely to attract larger mines (e.g., substantial oil sands and gold–copper mines) that require longer timelines needed for analysis, which may explain why they were not significantly different than federal timelines (Supplementary Material 6; Figs. S2 and S3).

We would have liked to compare to the _IAA 2019_ to other laws, but at the time of data collection, insufficient projects had completed assessment under the newer law. There has been significant federal government attention directed at reducing the time associated with environmental licensing, particularly for energy and mining projects associated with “clean growth” (Ministerial Working Group on Regulatory Efficiency for Clean Growth Projects 2024). Although they did not specifically investigate IA timelines, Collard et al. (2024) found that in British Columbia it is typically economic factors that drive post-IA delays to mine operations rather than licensing and permitting requirements. Research is needed to understand the relative contributions of regulations as contrasted with the labour force, production, and economic factors (including development costs and commodity pricing) to understand project approvals, rejections, and delays under the _IAA 2019_ and other laws.

### Moving towards a harmonized and clear IA system in Canada

Canada has a rich, albeit varied history of trying to achieve cooperation and reduce duplication of IA processes across its federal system (e.g., Kennett 1993; Fitzpatrick and Sinclair 2009; Fitzpatrick et al. 2024). Cooperation agreements were signed between seven provinces/territories and the federal government in the mid 2000s under _CEAA 1992_. Only British Columbia continued collaboration efforts with follow up agreements for IAs under _CEAA 2012_ and _IAA 2019_ (Impact Assessment Agency of Canada 2020).

The multi-jurisdictional legislative IA context in Canada resulted in some cases (15% of our database, _n_=39) where proponents set out to build one mine and triggered two simultaneous IAs. While a detailed investigation into each of these cases is outside the scope of our study, we found that these simultaneous and/or duplicated IAs showed considerable discrepancies in key metrics. British Columbia showed fewer discrepancies than other jurisdictions, potentially due to its cooperation agreements with the federal government that set the standards for IA substitution. Yet, serious misalignments remained: for example, the Prosperity Gold Mine was approved by British Columbia and rejected twice by the federal government (Mehdic et al. 2020; MacPhail et al. 2022; Wilson and Allard 2023). There were vast differences in key metrics for the eight mines assessed both in Québec and federally. Production rate for mines assessed both federally and in Québec differed by an average of 17 238 tonnes/day, over five times the baseline production capacity (3000 tonnes/day) for a large metal mine to trigger a federal IA under _CEAA 2012_.

One factor that may explain some of these cases is the differences in time at which various stages of the IA proceed—even differences of months to a single year may matter greatly. The economics of developing a large-scale mine are dynamic; over a period of days to months, production plans may change in response to economic factors like commodity pricing and geopolitics (Mishra and Mohanty 2020; Suárez Nieto et al. 2024). Meanwhile, IA might be proceeding with stakeholder and rightsholder input on an outdated project proposal. Economic feasibility studies are not explicitly mandated under most IA regimes in Canada (though proponents may elect to conduct one). Requiring economic feasibility studies before or during the IA process would help provide greater certainty and transparency around operational plans (Bullock and Mernitz 2017) which are undergoing impact predictions and community consultations.

The division of powers established in the Canadian constitution related to the environment generally (and therefore IA) has been subject to repeated attention by the Supreme Court of Canada. The most recent 2023 decision (_Reference re Impact Assessment Act, 2023 SCC 23_), reaffirmed earlier cases (_Friends of the Oldman River Society v. Canada (Minister of Transport), 1992 110 (SCC), [1992] 1 SCR 3_; _References re Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act, 2021 SCC 11, [2021] 1 SCR 175_) that found both the federal and provincial governments have jurisdiction over IA, but the application of _IAA 2019_ had, in certain areas, overstepped federal jurisdiction into provincial matters. In response to this reference case, the _IAA 2019_ was amended in 2024 to narrow its attention to effects within federal jurisdiction. In its conclusion, the SCC decision offers (paragraph 216): “it is open to Parliament and the provincial legislatures to exercise their respective powers over the environment harmoniously, in the spirit of cooperative federalism”.

We echo the spirit of this decision and encourage greater cooperation across Canada with respect to IA. Jurisdictional siloing, as framed by Johnston et al. (2025), poses challenges to best practices of IA which includes a holistic approach to cumulative effects assessment and efforts to ensure decisions are considered in the context of sustainability. Jurisdictional siloing also perpetuates uneven application of IA to proposed mines and quarries by fragmenting data records. Siloing paired with “project splitting” (when the assessing jurisdiction narrowly frames its review to separate project components; Doelle 2010; Enríquez-de-Salamanca 2016) can significantly hinder the ability for researchers and communities to compare proposed environmental and/or social impacts among and between projects. For example, the Lynn Lake Gold Project underwent duplicated IAs, both of which concluded in 2023, under the federal _CEAA 2012_ and Manitoba _EA 1988_. We could not compare the two sets of reported key project metrics between these two jurisdictions because the federal assessment examined the project in its entirety (Stantec Consulting Ltd. 2020 _a_), whereas the province split the project into two separate IAs: the Gordon pit (Stantec Consulting Ltd. 2020 _b_) and the MacLellan pit (Stantec Consulting Ltd. 2020 _c_). More attention must be paid to improving coordination and cooperation between the federal, provincial, territorial, and/or Indigenous governments engaged in IA (see Fitzpatrick et al. 2024; Johnston et al. 2025).

In 2025, international trade disputes and political shifts drew announcements from different levels of Canadian government regarding “fast-tracked” (Government of British Columbia 2025; Government of Ontario 2025), or “one-window” (Government of Canada 2025) IAs. These announcements have resulted in new laws being passed at national (_One Canadian Economy Act_, SC 2025, c 2) and subnational (_Protecting Ontario by Unleashing our Economy Act_, SO 2025, c 4; _Infrastructure Projects Act_, SBC 2025, c 13) levels, with streamlined permitting of mines—especially for critical minerals—as a common thread throughout (Deberdt and Letourneau 2025). How these laws are implemented, and if other provinces and territories follow suit with their own laws or policies to de-couple the practice of IA from mining development, remains to be seen. If jurisdictions wish to efficiently conduct mine and quarry IAs while striving for transparent and robust processes, they should follow three recommendations:

1.

Jurisdictions should clearly distinguish what types of mines (if any) are eligible for streamlined IA, and under what rationale. For example, if streamlining is geared towards the exploitation of critical minerals, regulators should outline explicit and measurable criteria for what projects this includes to avoid risking non-critical mines (e.g., gold mines that produce a small amount of copper) being lumped together with critical ones.

2.

Harmonization should be done in an _upwards_ fashion (Kwasniak 2009), meaning the more rigorous IA regime should be used if regulators truly intend to achieve the “highest standards for safety, environmental protection, and Indigenous consultation” (Government of Canada 2025). For example, IAs under Nova Scotia's _Environment Act_, SNS 1994-95, c 1 do not require cumulative effects to be considered; thus, an upwards-harmonized IA for a new mine in Nova Scotia would adopt the cumulative effects considerations (s. 22(1)) from the _IAA 2019_.

3.

Most importantly, harmonization and fast-tracking efforts need to ensure the duty to consult with Indigenous Peoples is executed fulsomely and in good faith (Booth and Skelton 2011; Craik 2015; Buchan 2019; Nishima-Miller et al. 2024), as well as meaningful public participation. This has been a barrier to past attempts to streamline IA (Mikadze 2016; Johnston 2024). For example, pipeline approvals under _CEAA 2012_ were overturned by courts on the basis of inadequate consultation of Indigenous peoples (_Gitxaala Nation v. Canada, 2016 FCA 187_; _Tsleil-Waututh Nation v. Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 153_). The recently passed streamlining laws are already receiving pushback, protests, and legal action from Indigenous groups and civil society actors (Chandler 2025; Chiefs of Ontario 2025; Jones 2025). Lessons from the near history suggest that a lack of meaningful consultation with rights-holders on new projects is likely to result in legal action that could delay project development for considerably longer than it would take to complete a rigorous project-level IA, or halt development entirely.

## Conclusion

We present a first-of-its-kind database of mines and quarries, which have undergone IA in jurisdictions across Canada. Due to the incompleteness of regulator registries, there are many data gaps in both the list of projects and the key metrics we extracted. Nevertheless, researchers can use our database to further elaborate on jurisdictional, economic, and policy trends. A particularly interesting question would be to examine the fate of these projects and audit how their built size, lifespan, and projections of economic and environmental impact aligned with what was proposed. Collard et al. (2023) have developed an IA auditing method that could be applied to our database, in combination with other datasets such as those that track mine closures (Dallaire-Fortier 2024 _b_).

Based on our findings, we have several recommendations for regulators. We encourage all jurisdictions to adopt the FAIR principles (Wilkinson et al. 2016) for data sharing of public records through both IA registries and mining recorders’ offices. Strides to increase data availability must respect the ownership, control, access, and possession (OCAP) principles and rights of Indigenous peoples who are involved with IAs or other forms of planning and decision-making processes (Eckert et al. 2020; Cannon et al. 2024; Corston et al. 2024). Regulators should, at minimum, ensure that project proponents report the key metrics of production size, footprint, and lifespan in major assessment documents (e.g., project description, EIS) with clear explanations for how these metrics are calculated. Ideally, these key metrics should be shared on registry landing pages for each project.

To support interoperability, we encourage regulators to cooperate with one another to standardize these metrics among project types. This could be accomplished by having regulators coordinate the information they request in the terms of reference that are given to project proponents at the outset of IA processes. Definitions of production size should be standardized within and between project classes (as feasible) with clearly specified units (e.g., tonnes of ore/day). Lifespan should distinguish between the proposed durations of each project phase (e.g., construction, operations, active closure, passive remediation, follow-up monitoring). At present, some projects only provide _footprint_ calculations based on major mine components (pits, processing facilities) while excluding utility/road corridors. Instead of the planned physical footprint, some proposals only reported a regional “study area” (e.g., project site+500 m buffer) and others only provided information on “disturbed habitat” for a particular species. How footprint is to be calculated should be clearly delineated in terms of reference and aligned across jurisdictions. Finally, as different levels of government continue to politicize discussions about IA timelines, jurisdictions should coordinate to standardize what event determines the “start” of an IA process. For example, in Alberta, the “start” is based on when an EIS is submitted, whereas in the federal process, the “start” begins when a (pre-EIS) project description is submitted.

To facilitate access to information, all jurisdictions’ online registries should be updated include search functions as well as the ability to filter by variables including the law under which a project was assessed, project class, target commodity, year ranges, and others. We encourage regulators to continue to make project documents accessible online, including digitizing paper records from past IAs. Some of Canada's IA agencies pride themselves on transparency and opportunities for public involvement (Gilmour and Stacey 2024), so we posit that digitizing files from historical IAs (usually already held within government purview) would be a proactive short-term minimal cost with long lasting benefits. We encountered significant roadblocks when engaging in FOI processes, and these processes have been criticized for not adequately supporting the public's right to information (Black 2023; Cardaso and Doolittle 2024; Laroche 2024). Jurisdictions should make sure their FOI processes are clear, easy to navigate, and to hold to their own prescribed timelines for responding to FOI requests.

Moving forward, legal and policy changes can support clearer and more aligned IA practices in Canada. This will become particularly important as Indigenous-led assessment becomes more common (First Nations Energy and Mining Council 2019; Bruce et al. 2024; [Nishima-Miller et al. 2024](https://www.facetsjournal.com/doi/full/10.1139/facets-2025

# International Association for Impact Assessment (IAIA)

The International Association for Impact Assessment (IAIA) is a global nongovernmental organization dedicated to advancing biodiversity protection and promoting sustainable development. With over 2,500 members across more than 100 countries, IAIA emphasizes free and open access to its environmental impact assessment projects, ensuring the use of current and unbiased research findings. IAIA conducts research across various departments, addressing areas such as agriculture, forestry, biodiversity, disaster response, corporate stewardship, and health impacts, all with a focus on enhancing environmental and human rights protections.

The organization actively engages in public participation for its assessments and promotes the integration of local knowledge, especially concerning indigenous communities. IAIA tracks environmental legislation globally and shares its findings through its professional journal, "Impact Assessment and Project Appraisal," which highlights best practices and relevant updates. Additionally, IAIA publishes methodology guides to support effective assessment practices, aligning its efforts with major international environmental agreements. Through these initiatives, IAIA seeks to foster informed decision-making that balances developmental needs with ecological sustainability.

## Full Article

*   **DATE:** Established 1980

_The International Association for Impact Assessment brings together researchers in the sciences and social sciences, policymakers, academics, and others to analyze the possible and probable consequences of development policies for the environmental, social, economic, and cultural health of human societies around the world._

### Background

The International Association for Impact Assessment (IAIA) is a nongovernmental organization dedicated to the protection of [biodiversity](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/science/biodiversity) and the promotion of [sustainable development](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/environmental-sciences/sustainable-development-overview) on a local to global scale. IAIA supports free and open access to all its environmental impact assessment projects, which use the most current, comprehensive, and unbiased research findings available. IAIA consists of more than 1,300 members in more than one hundred countries. All IAIA research projects aim to protect both the natural environment and [human rights](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/human-rights), while developing increasingly sophisticated environmental impact assessments.

### Impact on Resource Use

IAIA divides its members’ research projects into several departments. The agriculture, [forestry](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/forestry/forestry), and [fisheries](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/agriculture-and-agribusiness/fisheries-and-environmentalism) department collects data to develop numerous and widely available sustainable practices. The biodiversity and ecology department provides information to help establish environmentally significant and sensitive locations and develop ways to protect them. The disaster and conflict department collects information on the environmental impact of natural disasters, including the negative impact on biodiversity in affected areas. This helps develop environmentally and human-sensitive policy responses. The corporate stewardship department assists corporations in designing environmentally positive decisions in their manufacturing, marketing, and distribution processes. Trade-related projects focus on environmentally benign international and transnational trade development.

IAIA includes a department dedicated specifically to assessing the impact of development policies on Indigenous peoples and how best to preserve traditional forms of knowledge. The health impact department collects and disseminates information related to the connections between human health and environmental development and/or preservation. IAIA also tracks environmental impact legislation around the globe via its impact assessment law department.

All IAIA departments include options for public participation in environmental impact assessments and the provision of information helpful in constructing legislation in line with IAIA mission of environmentally aware development. IAIA publishes research findings, including requisite estimated cost-benefit analyses, in its professional journal, _Impact Assessment and Project Appraisal_. The journal also includes a [best practices](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/social-sciences-and-humanities/best-practices) section, book reviews, and updates on global environmental projects and legislation. Additionally, IAIA publishes numerous books on assessment methodologies to ensure that research findings are reported in the most credible and functional way for later use in drafting legislation or supporting policy decisions. These methodology texts include volumes on what to assess for biodiversity impact, how research samples must be constructed for social impact assessments, and options for developing corporate stewardship decisions. IAIA uses its publications to contribute to global sustainable development projects in line with the goals of the Ramsar Convention, the Convention on Biological Diversity, the World Water Forum, the Espoo Convention, and the Convention on Migratory Species.

*   **DATE:** Established 1980

_The International Association for Impact Assessment brings together researchers in the sciences and social sciences, policymakers, academics, and others to analyze the possible and probable consequences of development policies for the environmental, social, economic, and cultural health of human societies around the world._

### Background

The International Association for Impact Assessment (IAIA) is a nongovernmental organization dedicated to the protection of [biodiversity](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/science/biodiversity) and the promotion of [sustainable development](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/environmental-sciences/sustainable-development-overview) on a local to global scale. IAIA supports free and open access to all its environmental impact assessment projects, which use the most current, comprehensive, and unbiased research findings available. IAIA consists of more than 1,300 members in more than one hundred countries. All IAIA research projects aim to protect both the natural environment and [human rights](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/human-rights), while developing increasingly sophisticated environmental impact assessments.

### Impact on Resource Use

IAIA divides its members’ research projects into several departments. The agriculture, [forestry](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/forestry/forestry), and [fisheries](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/agriculture-and-agribusiness/fisheries-and-environmentalism) department collects data to develop numerous and widely available sustainable practices. The biodiversity and ecology department provides information to help establish environmentally significant and sensitive locations and develop ways to protect them. The disaster and conflict department collects information on the environmental impact of natural disasters, including the negative impact on biodiversity in affected areas. This helps develop environmentally and human-sensitive policy responses. The corporate stewardship department assists corporations in designing environmentally positive decisions in their manufacturing, marketing, and distribution processes. Trade-related projects focus on environmentally benign international and transnational trade development.

IAIA includes a department dedicated specifically to assessing the impact of development policies on Indigenous peoples and how best to preserve traditional forms of knowledge. The health impact department collects and disseminates information related to the connections between human health and environmental development and/or preservation. IAIA also tracks environmental impact legislation around the globe via its impact assessment law department.

All IAIA departments include options for public participation in environmental impact assessments and the provision of information helpful in constructing legislation in line with IAIA mission of environmentally aware development. IAIA publishes research findings, including requisite estimated cost-benefit analyses, in its professional journal, _Impact Assessment and Project Appraisal_. The journal also includes a [best practices](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/social-sciences-and-humanities/best-practices) section, book reviews, and updates on global environmental projects and legislation. Additionally, IAIA publishes numerous books on assessment methodologies to ensure that research findings are reported in the most credible and functional way for later use in drafting legislation or supporting policy decisions. These methodology texts include volumes on what to assess for biodiversity impact, how research samples must be constructed for social impact assessments, and options for developing corporate stewardship decisions. IAIA uses its publications to contribute to global sustainable development projects in line with the goals of the Ramsar Convention, the Convention on Biological Diversity, the World Water Forum, the Espoo Convention, and the Convention on Migratory Species.

## Abstract

Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is applied to infrastructure and other large projects. The European Union EIA Directive (2011/92/EU as amended by 2014/52/EU) requires EIAs to consider the effects that a project might have on human health. The International Association for Impact Assessment and the European Public Health Association prepared a reference paper on public health in EIA to enable the health sector to contribute to this international requirement. We present lessons from this joint action. We review literature on policy analysis, impact assessment and Health Impact Assessment (HIA). We use findings from this review and from the consultation on the reference paper to consider how population and human health should be defined; how the health sector can participate in the EIA process; the relationship between EIA and HIA; what counts as evidence; when an effect should be considered ‘likely’ and ‘significant’; how changes in health should be reported; the risks from a business-as-usual coverage of human health in EIA; and finally competencies for conducting an assessment of human health. This article is relevant for health authorities seeking to ensure that infrastructure, and other aspects of development, are not deleterious to, but indeed improve, human health.

**Keywords:**Environmental Impact Assessment, human health, public health, Health Impact Assessment, Health in All Policies, significance, equity, health inequality, infrastructure

## 1. Introduction

We present lessons from drafting a technical reference paper [1] for health in Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA). From a core health sector perspective, this is quite a niche topic and yet EIA is a very important regulatory mechanism. In 2018, the UN Environment Programme [2] stated that EIA is the most commonly known, most commonly used, and globally widespread, environmental planning and management tool and that it is the only environmental policy tool that is required by most countries around the world and whose results are regularly publicly acknowledged and available. EIA is established in international and national law but it is applied at the local level and involves local government, civil society and the private sector. The theory and methods that inform EIA permeate thinking in spatial planning.

The broader context for this article is the way in which public health is considered in policy making, both in and outside of the health sector. This has direct relevance for Health in All Policies (HiAP) as it examines ways in which reasoning for public health is presented in a regulatory context outside the health sector. We paraphrase Morgan’s [3] wise observation that impact assessment practitioners and public health specialists have much to learn from one another and we look at topics such as the nature of evidence, the relative merits of quantitative versus qualitative methods, coping with uncertainty, the role, and effective use, of public participation, and evaluating social significance. This article has specific relevance for health authorities seeking to ensure that infrastructure, and other aspects of development, are not deleterious to, and indeed improve, public health.

### 1.1. Background

EIA is governed in the European Union (EU) by Directive 2011/92/EU on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment [4], as amended by 2014/52/EU [5] (hereafter the ‘EIA Directive’). The amendments made in 2014 include a stipulation that human health is considered when conducting EIA. Recital 41 of EU Directive 2014/52/EU states that the objective of EIA [is] to ensure a high level of protection of the environment and of human health.

In 2018, a joint action was initiated by the International Association for Impact Assessment (IAIA) and the European Public Health Association (EUPHA) to prepare a reference paper on health in EIA [1] and to set out ways in which the health sector can contribute to this regulatory requirement. A reference paper is a formal document that provides additional content which is relevant to existing commitments [6]. Reference papers tend to be non-binding but they can assist agencies in formulating approaches to a topic [7] and parties to an agreement can adopt them if they so choose [6]. They are often written before practices develop ‘by default’ into standards [8]. We present key findings from writing this reference paper. We start by introducing EIA and the amendments to the EIA Directive. We set out the materials and methods for this study and, in the discussion, we navigate the literature on policy analysis, Health Impact Assessment (HIA) and health in other forms of impact assessment. Whilst the reference paper is structured around the EIA Directive, the principles and approaches it discusses have global application to health in impact assessment.

### 1.2. Environmental Impact Assessment

EIA is a regulatory mechanism that was first introduced in the United States by the National Environmental Policy Act in 1969 [9] and it is now in place in many countries across the world. EIA is applied to projects such as transport infrastructure, residential development, infrastructure for processing waste materials and infrastructure for generating, transmitting and storing energy. These projects are typically large, with lasting effects on the environment. The European Commission states that the EIA Directive is a crucial tool for sustainable development [10]. The EIA Directive has currency outside the twenty-seven Member States because the financial institutions of the EU such as the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and the European Investment Bank (EIB) ensure that projects to which they advance loans apply the EIA Directive when conducting environmental assessments [11,12].

The process of EIA is designed to sustain environmental values when developments that might compromise those values are proposed [13]. Box 1 shows the EIA process as set out in Article 1(2)(g) of the EIA Directive. (see Box 1).

There is a large but often well-defined cast of actors, or stakeholders, that take part in an EIA. The party that is seeking consent for a project will prepare an EIA Report. This party is typically referred to as the developer.

#### Box 1. The EIA process as set out in Article 1(2)(g) of the EIA Directive. From Directive 2011/92/EU as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU [5].

For the purposes of this Directive, the following definitions shall apply:

[…]

(g)‘environmental impact assessment’ means a process consisting of:

(i)the preparation of an environmental impact assessment report by the developer, as referred to in Article 5(1) and (2);(ii)the carrying out of consultations as referred to in Article 6 and, where relevant, Article 7;(iii)the examination by the competent authority of the information presented in the environmental impact assessment report and any supplementary information provided, where necessary, by the developer in accordance with Article 5(3), and any relevant information received through the consultations under Articles 6 and 7;(iv)the reasoned conclusion by the competent authority on the significant effects of the project on the environment, taking into account the results of the examination referred to in point (iii) and, where appropriate, its own supplementary examination; and(v)the integration of the competent authority’s reasoned conclusion into any of the decisions referred to in Article 8a.

The EIA Report is examined by the competent authority which is the department of planning or the environmental regulator in a given geographic area. The competent authority then reaches a reasoned conclusion based on its examination of the developer’s EIA Report as well as the consultation responses, other documents submitted by the developer in support of the application and, where appropriate, the results of its own supplementary examination. Developers will often use private sector consultants to ensure they have expert advice on each of the topics listed in Article 3 (see Box 2).

The solutions proposed in the EIA tend to be avoidance or mitigation of adverse effects. Each assessment focusses upon effects that are both likely and significant (as per Article 5 (1)b). Attention is thus paid to identifying these potential adverse effects, and then finding ways in which to ensure that they do not occur. This is usually achieved by adapting the design of the project or reaching an agreement between the developer and the relevant authorities/stakeholders for measures to counteract, or mitigate, the adverse effects. These aspects are then monitored. EIA is a regulatory process so the changes to design and the agreed measures are set out in formal and binding agreements and will typically be funded by the developer.

### 1.3. Why Is the Amended EIA Directive Relevant to Human Health and to the Health Sector?

The 2014 amendments were transposed into the regulations of each EU Member State in 2017 [14]. The amendments are extensive, they affect most of the pre-existing legislation [15,16] and have considerable implications for EIA practice. Commentators note how the amendments require a focus on the quality of content in the EIA, on timeliness and relevance of reporting as well as monitoring project compliance [17]; how regards must be given to the potential effects of any different, or ‘alternative’, design scenarios that were considered [18] and how decision makers are required to engage with the public [19].

The main change, from a health perspective, is the inclusion of _human health_ among the topics to be considered in EIA (see Box 2). It is this that brings the health sector into the orbit of EIA.

#### Box 2. Text of Article 3 in the amended EIA Directive 2014/52 EU. From Directive 2011/92/EU as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU [5].

1.The environmental impact assessment shall identify, describe and assess in an appropriate manner, in the light of each individual case, the direct and indirect significant effects of a project on the following factors: (a)population and human health;(b)biodiversity, with particular attention to species and habitats protected under Directive 92/43/EEC and Directive 2009/147/EC;(c)land, soil, water, air and climate;(d)material assets, cultural heritage and the landscape;(e)the interaction between the factors referred to in points (a) to (d).

2.The effects referred to in paragraph 1 on the factors set out therein shall include the expected effects deriving from the vulnerability of the project to risks of major accidents and/or disasters that are relevant to the project concerned.

Other topics are also introduced by the amendments: climate change mitigation and adaptation, accidents and disasters, land and biodiversity [18] (see Box 2). Hough [19] notes that expanding the factors to be considered will increase the workload of, and complexity in, preparing an EIA Report and that it can be expected to result in longer documents and a greater workload for impact assessors and public authorities. Mustow [20] notes that substantial changes in impact assessment practice are required to incorporate human health assessment. Change is not a problem in itself as EIA practice in Europe has been constantly developing since Directive 1985/337/EEC [21] made it mandatory for members of the European Economic Community. The 2014 amendments introduce human health as a new consideration and we look below at the implications of involving the health sector in the EIA process.

## 2. Materials and Methods

A writing team convened in September 2018. This team was consisted of members of the health section of IAIA and the HIA section of EUPHA. The World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Europe provided support in the early stages. From the inception to the publication, in December 2020, there were three drafts of the reference paper and four consultation ‘events’ (see Figure 1) and the writing team met approximately 30 times.

The reference paper examines the EIA Directive and European Commission guidance on EIA [22,23,24] and regional and national guidance for health in EIA for example [25,26,27,28]. It complements guidance for HIA for example, [29,30] and it is informed by international good practice [31,32,33,34,35]. It builds on previous work conducted jointly, and separately, by IAIA, EUPHA and the WHO Regional Office for Europe [36,37,38]. It also draws on the literature on policy analysis, HIA and health in other forms of impact assessment and the experience of the writing team gained over two decades on work in public health and impact assessment.

The first draft of the reference paper was discussed in March 2019, at a technical meeting hosted by the European Centre for Environmental and Health at the WHO Regional Office for Europe in Bonn. Participants examined questions that had been identified through the practice of HIA, of health in EIA and the application of the amended EIA Directive. These are provided below and were first set out in Cave et al. [27] as questions to which the health sector in general, and public health in particular, needs to develop consensus to enable consideration of health in EIA.

1.   How should population and human health be defined in EIA?

2.   How should the health sector participate in the EIA process?

3.   What is the relationship between EIA and HIA?

4.   What counts as evidence for changes in health?

5.   When is an effect ‘likely’ and ‘significant’?

6.   How should potential changes in health be reported?

7.   What are the risks from a business-as-usual coverage of population and human health in EIA?

8.   Who can conduct an assessment?

The subsequent consultation events invited comment on substantive issues to do with health in EIA and they also asked consultees about the clarity, structure, accessibility, etc. of the reference paper. The second draft was consulted upon, from November 2019 to January 2020, via a webinar and a survey hosted by IAIA. The third draft of the reference paper was peer reviewed, in March 2020, by three referees drawn from IAIA members before being finalized and then published in December of 2020. The draft reference paper was amended after each of these consultations.

A thematic coding strategy was applied to the comments provided in the consultation processes. This identified themes such as target audience of the reference paper; health determinants; significance/likely health effect; equity/vulnerable groups; methods/tools; role of public health professionals/competences needed; intersectoral cooperation/stakeholders/responsible authorities. The responses given to the survey and the peer-review comments were based upon a reading of the second and third drafts, respectively, of the reference paper and so these comments were also analyzed with the framework identified by Herber et al. [39] which relates to peer review of a qualitative manuscript. Details about the consultation and the responses are provided in the supplementary information (Supplementary Materials File S1).
